courses.title: AI Agents at Work
courses.description: Hand multi-step work to an AI agent with clear goals and limits, then supervise it and approve the result before anything leaves your hands.

lessons.goal: Explain what an AI agent does and pick tasks that suit one.
lessons.title: From chat to agents

blocks.title: Chat answers, agents act
blocks.body: In a chat, you ask and the assistant replies once. An **agent** works toward a goal. It plans steps, uses tools such as web browsing, your files or workplace apps, checks what it finds and continues until it thinks the goal is met. Unlike a fixed flow, it chooses its own steps; you describe the outcome.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.body: Goal: "Collect last month's competitor price changes from their public pages and put them in a table." The agent opens each page, compares them with your file and builds the table. In chat, you would copy every page by hand.

blocks.title: Which tasks suit an agent
blocks.body: Good fits have many steps, clear inputs and a result you can check: research, recurring reports, data gathering. Poor fits need personal judgment, handle sensitive decisions or cannot be undone. Agents can misread pages, so you stay responsible for the result.

blocks.question: What mainly separates an agent from a normal chat reply?
options: It plans several steps and uses tools to work toward a goal.
It is always correct because it checks itself.
It answers faster than a chat assistant.
It needs no instructions from you.
blocks.explanation: An agent acts across steps with tools. It still makes mistakes and needs a clear goal.
blocks.hint: What happens between your request and its result?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which tasks suit an agent?
options: Gathering public pricing from ten websites into a table.
Compiling the weekly sales report from the same sources each Monday.
Deciding which employee gets a promotion.
Finding and listing public sources on a new regulation.
blocks.explanation: These have many steps and a result you can check. A promotion is a sensitive judgment that stays with you.
blocks.hint: Look for tasks with checkable results, not personal decisions.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: An agent can use tools such as browsing or files.
cards.explanation: Tools are what let it act beyond writing text.

cards.statement: If an agent finishes, the result is verified.
cards.explanation: Finishing only means it believes it is done. You still check.

cards.statement: A task you cannot undo is a poor first task for an agent.
cards.explanation: Mistakes cost more when nothing can be reversed.

blocks.hint: Ask what happens if the agent is wrong.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that turns this chat request into an agent goal.
blocks.prompt: Research our three main competitors. ___
options: Tell me what you know about them.
Open their public pricing pages and list each plan and price in a table, with the page link.
Be thorough.
blocks.explanation: It names the sources, the result and the format, so you can check each row.
blocks.hint: Which option describes work in outside sources, not memory?

blocks.question: Which task is the best first one to give an agent?
options: Sending a refund decision to a customer.
Collecting this week's public job postings from three sites into a list.
Deleting old files from the shared drive.
Choosing which supplier to sign with.
blocks.explanation: It is repeatable, reads public data and the result is easy to review. The others act or decide.
blocks.hint: Prefer reading and collecting over sending, deleting or deciding.

practice.instructions: Choose one repeating task from your work that suits an agent and one that does not, and explain why.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Name one task related to this pain that suits an agent in {{tool}} or a workplace agent, and one that does not. For each, say what steps are involved, what the agent would use and what could go wrong.

rubric.description: The task has several steps, clear inputs and a result that can be checked.
The second task involves sensitive judgment or cannot be undone, and the learner says why.
The learner names a realistic error and how they would notice it.

practice.example_good_prompt: Suits an agent: each Monday, open our five suppliers' public news pages and list new announcements with links. Steps: visit, read, summarize; it needs browsing. Risk: it may miss or misread a page, so I spot-check two links. Does not suit: deciding which supplier to drop, because that is a judgment with business consequences.

common_mistakes: Learners think an agent is just a smarter chat. Ask what tools it would use and what steps it would take.
Learners pick high-stakes first tasks. Steer them to reading and collecting tasks.
key_points: An agent plans steps and uses tools toward a goal.
Good tasks are multi-step, repeatable and checkable.
You stay responsible for the result.

lessons.goal: Write a delegation brief with a goal, inputs, boundaries and a definition of done.
lessons.title: Delegate a task well

blocks.title: Four parts of a brief
blocks.body: Treat an agent like a new colleague. Give it a **goal** (the outcome and why), **inputs** (files, links, data to use), **boundaries** (what it may and may not do) and **done** (what the result looks like). Vague goals make an agent guess.

blocks.title: Boundaries and access
blocks.body: Give access only to what the task needs. A research task needs public web pages, not your inbox. Say what is off limits: "Read only. Do not send, edit, buy or delete anything. If you need something else, stop and ask me." Keep confidential data out unless your company approves the tool.

blocks.title: Example brief
blocks.body: "Goal: compare three competitor plans for Friday's pricing meeting. Inputs: our price list file, three public pricing pages. Boundaries: public pages only, read only, no sign-ups. Done: one table with plan, price and page link, plus a list of anything you could not verify."

blocks.question: Which brief is best for an agent?
options: Look into our competitors.
Goal: list three competitors' plans for Friday's meeting. Use these public pages only. Done: a table with prices and links.
Do whatever you need to find their prices.
Research competitors and email the team when ready.
blocks.explanation: It gives a goal, inputs, a boundary and a clear end result. The others leave steps or access open.
blocks.hint: Which option covers all four parts?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which boundaries make sense for a research agent?
options: Use public web pages only.
Read only: do not send, buy or delete anything.
Ask me before using any other source.
Full access to my email so it has context.
blocks.explanation: Limited access and a duty to ask reduce harm if the agent errs. Email access is not needed for this task.
blocks.hint: Which options reduce what the agent can touch?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that defines "done" best.
blocks.prompt: Prepare the weekly sales summary from the attached export. ___
options: Finish when it looks good.
Done means one page: total sales, top three products and any week-on-week drop above 10 percent.
Make it complete.
blocks.explanation: A concrete result lets the agent stop at the right point and lets you check it quickly.
blocks.hint: Which result could you check quickly?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Give the agent broad access now so you do not need to adjust it later.
cards.explanation: Broad access increases the damage a mistake can cause.

cards.statement: Telling the agent to stop and ask when unsure is a useful boundary.
cards.explanation: It prevents guesses on unclear steps.

cards.statement: Personal data can go to any agent tool without a check.
cards.explanation: Use only tools your company approves for that data.

blocks.hint: Ask what is the smallest access that still finishes the task.

blocks.question: You want an agent to gather candidate questions from a public forum. Which access is right?
options: Read-only web browsing.
Browsing plus access to the applicant tracking system.
Browsing plus permission to post replies.
Browsing plus access to the whole shared drive.
blocks.explanation: Gathering needs only reading. Extra access adds risk and exposes candidate data.
blocks.hint: Compare each option with what the task actually requires.

practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a brief for an agent in {{tool}} or a workplace agent that handles one task related to this pain. Include the goal, the inputs, what it may and may not access or do, and what done looks like. Use no confidential data.
practice.default_context: You are an office manager who needs a table of three suppliers' public delivery terms before Friday.

rubric.description: States the outcome, the purpose and which sources or files to use.
Says what is allowed and forbidden, limits access to what the task needs and asks it to stop when unsure.
Describes the result's format and what to flag as unverified.

practice.example_good_prompt: Goal: compare delivery terms of suppliers A, B and C for Friday's review. Inputs: their public terms pages. Boundaries: public pages only, read only, no sign-ups or emails; stop and ask if a page needs login. Done: one table with supplier, delivery time, cost and link, plus a list of anything unclear.

common_mistakes: Briefs with a goal but no boundaries. Ask what the agent must never do.
Granting wide access for convenience. Ask what the task truly needs.
key_points: Goal, inputs, boundaries, done.
Minimal access for the task.
Tell the agent to stop and ask when unsure.

lessons.goal: Review an agent's steps and sources, approve risky actions yourself and tighten your instructions after a failure.
lessons.title: Supervise and review

blocks.title: Check the steps, not just the result
blocks.body: Agents can misread a page, skip a source or fill a gap with a guess. Ask for a short log of what it did and open the sources behind key facts. The log can be wrong too. Spot-check a few rows. If the first steps look wrong, stop early instead of waiting for the final result.

blocks.title: You approve the irreversible
blocks.body: Require your approval before anything is **sent, paid or deleted**, or shared outside the company. Let the agent prepare drafts, orders or lists, then you review and press the button. Start small and widen only after it proves reliable.

blocks.title: Learn from failures
blocks.body: When a result is wrong, find the step where it went off. Was the goal unclear, the source weak or a boundary missing? Add that line to your brief, for example "Use only pages updated this year", and run again. A tighter brief is the fix, not more trust.

blocks.question: An agent's table lists a competitor price with no link. What do you do?
options: Use it, because the rest of the table looks fine.
Ask for the source link and open it before using the number.
Ask the agent if it is sure.
Delete the row and say nothing.
blocks.explanation: A figure without a source cannot be checked. Asking if it is sure does not verify anything.
blocks.hint: Where could you confirm the number yourself?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which actions should wait for your approval?
options: Sending a message to a client.
Paying a supplier invoice.
Deleting old files.
Reading a public web page.
blocks.explanation: Sending, paying and deleting are hard to undo. Reading a public page is low risk.
blocks.hint: Which actions are hard to reverse?

blocks.question: Pick the instruction that makes supervision easier.
blocks.prompt: Collect the data and build the report. ___
options: Work quietly and tell me when finished.
List the steps you took and the source of each figure, and stop before sending anything.
Send it to the team when ready.
blocks.explanation: A log and sources let you review, and stopping keeps the decision with you.
blocks.hint: Which option leaves you able to check and decide?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: After a failure, add the missing boundary or detail to your brief.
cards.explanation: A tighter brief prevents the same mistake.

cards.statement: A good agent run means you can stop checking sources.
cards.explanation: Reliability can change with the task and sources, so keep spot-checking.

cards.statement: You can widen the agent's tasks gradually as it proves reliable.
cards.explanation: Small steps limit the cost of early mistakes.

blocks.hint: Ask what you learn from each run.

blocks.question: An agent used an outdated page for its figures. What is the best fix?
options: Switch to a different agent tool.
Rerun it unchanged and hope for better luck.
Add to the brief: use only pages updated this year, and list the date of each source.
Fix the figures yourself and leave the brief alone.
blocks.explanation: Naming the missing rule and asking for dates prevents the error and makes it visible next time.
blocks.hint: Which option changes the instructions?

practice.instructions: Write a review plan for an agent run and a revised brief line after a failure.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. An agent in {{tool}} or a workplace agent will handle a task related to this pain. Write what you will check during and after the run, which actions need your approval, and one line you would add to the brief after the agent used a weak source.
practice.default_context: You are an office manager. An agent compiled supplier delivery terms, and one figure came from an outdated page.

rubric.description: Names specific checks such as the step log, source links or spot-checked rows.
Requires approval before sending, paying or deleting, and names which actions apply.
Adds a concrete instruction that addresses the failure.

practice.example_good_prompt: I will ask for a step log and a link and date for every figure, and open three links myself. The agent must stop before sending anything; I approve all emails and orders. After the outdated page I add: use only official pages updated this year and flag any source older than 12 months.

common_mistakes: Judging only the final result. Ask what the agent did to get there.
Letting the agent send or delete directly. Ask who presses the button.
key_points: Check steps and sources, not only the output.
Approve anything sent, paid or deleted.
Fix failures by tightening the brief.
follow_up_tasks: Take one past AI result and list which steps you would have wanted to see.

courses.title: AI Assistants 101
courses.description: Use an AI assistant for everyday office tasks, write clear prompts, refine the results and check them before you rely on them.

lessons.goal: Decide which AI answers you can use as they are and which facts you must check first.
lessons.title: Know what to trust and what to check

blocks.title: What assistants do well
blocks.body: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are strong with language. They draft emails, summarize documents, change the tone of a text and suggest report structures. Given text to work with, they usually produce a solid first draft.

blocks.title: Where they fail
blocks.body: An assistant predicts likely words. It can state a wrong date, a fake source or an invented policy with full confidence. This is called a **hallucination**. Even when it searches the web, it can misread what it finds. Its knowledge can also be out of date.

blocks.title: Check what matters
blocks.body: Ask: what happens if this is wrong? A friendly tone is low risk. A deadline, figure or legal reference in a client email is high risk, so check it at the source. Do not paste confidential or personal data into a personal or public AI tool. Use only tools your company approves.

blocks.question: An assistant gives a precise market growth figure for your client report. What do you do?
options: Use it, because a precise number sounds reliable.
Ask the assistant if it is sure, and use it if it says yes.
Find the figure in the original source first.
Round the number so a small error will not matter.
blocks.explanation: Assistants sound certain even when wrong. Asking again is not a check.
blocks.hint: Where would a trustworthy number be published?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which tasks suit an assistant as a first draft?
options: Rewriting a rough update more politely.
Summarizing meeting notes you paste in.
Stating the current legal deadline for a filing.
Suggesting an outline for a training guide.
blocks.explanation: These tasks use text you provide or structure, and you can judge the result yourself. A legal deadline is a fact you must verify.
blocks.hint: Look for tasks where you can judge the result yourself.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: An assistant can invent a source that does not exist.
cards.explanation: Fake references are a common hallucination. Open every source it cites.

cards.statement: A confident tone means the answer is correct.
cards.explanation: The tone is the same whether it is right or wrong.

cards.statement: An assistant's knowledge can be out of date.
cards.explanation: It may miss recent changes, so check anything time-sensitive.

blocks.hint: Ask whether the claim would still hold if the assistant were guessing.

blocks.question: Which line in an AI-written client email needs your check most?
options: Thank you for your patience.
Your contract renews on 14 March at the agreed rate.
Please let me know if you have questions.
I look forward to your reply.
blocks.explanation: A date and a rate are facts with consequences. The other lines are polite phrases.
blocks.hint: Which line could cause a problem if wrong?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt safest.
blocks.prompt: Draft a reminder to a customer about an overdue invoice. ___
options: Here is their full name, address and account number.
Use the placeholders [Name] and [Amount]; I will fill them in.
Look up what they owe in your records.
blocks.explanation: Placeholders keep personal data out of the tool. You add the real details yourself.
blocks.hint: What can you leave out of the prompt and add later?

practice.instructions: Ask your assistant to help with a real task, then list which parts of its answer you would check and why.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that asks for a first draft of a text related to this pain, without any confidential data. Then name two facts or claims in a likely answer that you would verify, and where you would check each one.
practice.default_context: You are an office coordinator who must write a short update for a client about a delayed delivery.

rubric.description: The prompt requests a clear draft or summary, not final facts.
The prompt uses placeholders or general wording instead of private details.
The learner lists specific claims to verify and a real source for each.

practice.example_good_prompt: Draft a short, polite update to a client about a delayed delivery. Use [Client] and [New date] as placeholders. Afterwards I will check the new date with our logistics team and the refund terms against the signed contract.

common_mistakes: Learners trust a precise number or citation. Steer them to ask where it would be confirmed.
Learners paste real names or figures. Show placeholders and ask what their company allows.
key_points: Assistants predict text, so they can sound sure and be wrong.
Check anything where an error has consequences.
Keep confidential data out of public tools.
follow_up_tasks: Take a short AI-written paragraph and mark every fact that needs a source.

lessons.goal: Write a prompt with role, context, task, format and constraints.
lessons.title: Write a prompt that gets a usable draft

blocks.title: Five parts of a prompt
blocks.body: A strong prompt answers five questions. **Role:** who should the assistant act as? **Context:** what is the situation and who reads it? **Task:** what exactly should it do? **Format:** what should the result look like? **Constraints:** what tone, length or facts apply?

blocks.title: Example
blocks.body:
Weak: "Write an email about the late report."

Better: "You are a project manager. A colleague's report is two days late and the client meeting is Friday. Write an email asking for it by Thursday noon. Keep it under 80 words, friendly but clear. No blame."

blocks.title: Why it works
blocks.body: The assistant cannot read your mind. Every missing detail becomes a guess, and guesses sound generic. You do not need all five parts every time. Add the ones that change the result, and always state the format and any facts it must use.

blocks.question: Which prompt is most likely to give a usable result?
options: Write a message to the team about the new schedule.
Write a good message about the schedule, make it professional.
Write a 4-sentence message to my team about the new Monday 9:00 stand-up. Friendly tone, ask them to confirm by Friday.
Team message, schedule, short.
blocks.explanation: It names the audience, task, length, tone and the action required. The others leave the assistant to guess.
blocks.hint: Count how many details each prompt gives.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which are parts of a well-built prompt?
options: Role
Context
Output format
Real names and personal details of everyone involved
blocks.explanation: Role, context and format shape the answer. Personal details are not needed and should stay out of the prompt.
blocks.hint: Choose what shapes the answer without adding risk.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that adds a useful output format.
blocks.prompt: Summarize these meeting notes for my manager. ___ Use plain language.
options: Make it great.
Give 3 bullet points, then one line on decisions we still need.
Do it quickly.
blocks.explanation: It tells the assistant the structure and length, so the summary is easy to scan.
blocks.hint: Which option describes what the result looks like?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Telling the assistant who will read the text helps it choose the right tone.
cards.explanation: Audience is context. A note to a client reads differently from one to a teammate.

cards.statement: A longer prompt is always a better prompt.
cards.explanation: Only details that change the result help. Padding adds noise.

cards.statement: Asking for a specific length helps you get a usable draft.
cards.explanation: A length limit stops long, vague answers.

cards.statement: If you skip the facts, the assistant will use your real data.
cards.explanation: It cannot see your files unless you provide the content, so it will guess.

blocks.hint: Ask whether the detail gives the assistant something to work with.

blocks.question: Which constraint best protects a customer email from errors?
options: Use these details only: refund of the amount below, 5 working days. Do not promise anything else.
Be accurate.
Sound smart.
Add more details to make it convincing.
blocks.explanation: Giving the facts and limiting what it may add keeps invented promises out of your email.
blocks.hint: Look for the option that limits what the assistant may invent.

practice.instructions: Write one prompt for a real task that includes role, context, task, format and constraints.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that helps with this, using role, context, task, output format and at least one constraint. Do not include confidential data.
practice.default_context: You are an office manager who must write a message asking staff to submit expense reports by month end.

rubric.description: States who the assistant is, the situation and the reader.
Asks for a format, length or structure.
Gives tone, facts to include or things to avoid, without private data.

practice.example_good_prompt: You are an office manager. Staff must submit expense reports by 30 June. Write a friendly email of 80 words or fewer, with a clear subject line, that explains the deadline and where to send reports. Use [Name] as a placeholder. Do not mention penalties.

common_mistakes: Prompts that say only "write an email". Ask who reads it and what they should do.
Skipping the format. Ask what the result should look like.
key_points: Role, context, task, format and constraints remove guesswork.
Always state the facts it must use.
Keep personal data out.
follow_up_tasks: Rewrite the weak prompt "summarize this report" using all five parts.

lessons.goal: Refine an AI draft with follow-up prompts and ask it to critique its own answer.
lessons.title: Improve the answer instead of starting over

blocks.title: Follow up, don't restart
blocks.body: The first answer is a draft. If something is off, say what to change. "Shorter, and lead with the deadline." The assistant keeps the conversation, so you keep what worked. Starting over throws away the context you built.

blocks.title: One change at a time
blocks.body: Name the problem, then the fix. "The tone is too formal. Rewrite it as if talking to a colleague I know well." Specific feedback works. "Make it better" does not, because the assistant has to guess what better means to you.

blocks.title: Ask for a critique
blocks.body: Ask: "Review your answer. What could be wrong, unclear or missing?" This often finds gaps. It is not proof. The assistant can miss its own mistakes, so you still check key facts. Stop when the draft meets your goal.

blocks.question: The assistant's summary is accurate but too long. What is the best next step?
options: Open a new chat and write the original prompt again.
Reply: Cut this to 5 bullet points, keep the dates.
Reply: Make it better.
Write the summary yourself.
blocks.explanation: A specific follow-up keeps what is good and changes only the length and format.
blocks.hint: Pick the reply that names exactly what to change.

blocks.question: Pick the follow-up that asks for a useful self-check.
blocks.prompt: Here is your draft of the client proposal. ___
options: Are you sure?
List any claims that might be wrong or need a source, and anything missing for a first-time client.
Rewrite the whole proposal from scratch.
blocks.explanation: A clear request for risks and gaps gives you a list of things to check.
blocks.hint: Which option asks for something concrete you can act on?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which follow-ups are specific enough to improve a draft?
options: Make the opening shorter and mention the deadline first.
Change the tone to friendly, but keep the figures.
Do it again.
Add one sentence thanking them for the quick reply.
blocks.explanation: Each one names a change. "Do it again" gives no direction.
blocks.hint: Look for the replies that say what to change.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If the assistant reviews its own answer and finds nothing wrong, you can skip checking.
cards.explanation: It can miss its own errors. Verify key facts yourself.

cards.statement: You can keep a good draft and ask to change just one part.
cards.explanation: Follow-ups let you adjust a single part without losing the rest.

cards.statement: Starting a fresh chat is always better than a follow-up.
cards.explanation: A fresh chat loses the context. Restart only if the conversation is off track.

cards.statement: You should stop when the draft meets your goal.
cards.explanation: More rounds can make text worse or longer without helping.

blocks.hint: Think about what keeps the useful context and what still needs your judgment.

blocks.question: After three rounds your email is clear, polite and correct. What next?
options: Keep asking for small tweaks until it feels perfect.
Check the facts, make final edits yourself and send it.
Start again to compare.
Ask the assistant to approve it.
blocks.explanation: When it meets the goal, stop. Your final check on facts and names is what makes it safe to send.
blocks.hint: Who is responsible for what goes out under your name?

practice.instructions: Write two follow-up prompts that improve a first AI draft, and one that asks the assistant to critique it.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. {{tool}} gave you a first draft of a message about this pain. It is too long and too formal. Write two specific follow-up prompts to fix this, then one prompt asking the assistant to point out risks or gaps.
practice.default_context: An assistant drafted a 300-word email to a client about a schedule change. It is too long and too formal.

rubric.description: Each follow-up names a clear change such as length, tone or structure.
Follow-ups build on the draft and do not ask to restart.
One prompt asks for risks, gaps or unsupported claims, and the learner plans to check facts.

practice.example_good_prompt: 1) Cut this to 100 words and lead with the new date. 2) Make the tone friendly, like writing to a colleague, and keep the figures. 3) Review the draft: which claims could be wrong, and what would a client want to know that is missing? I will then check the figures myself.

common_mistakes: Replies like "make it better". Ask what exactly should change.
Treating the self-critique as proof. Remind them to verify facts.
key_points: Refine with specific follow-ups.
A self-critique finds gaps but does not replace checking.
Stop when the draft meets the goal.
follow_up_tasks: Take one draft and improve it in two rounds, one change per round.

courses.title: AI for HR Teams
courses.description: Use an AI assistant to write fairer job ads and interview questions, simplify onboarding and policy materials, and analyze employee feedback without exposing personal data.

lessons.goal: Draft a job description and interview questions with AI, and check them for biased wording.
lessons.title: Fairer job ads and interview questions

blocks.title: Start with the real job
blocks.body: Give the assistant the role, the actual daily duties and the true must-have skills. Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves. Long wish lists put off strong candidates who only apply when they match every line. Never paste personal details about current staff into the prompt.

blocks.title: Ask AI to flag biased wording
blocks.body: Ask: "Review this job ad for biased or exclusionary wording and suggest neutral alternatives." Phrases like "young and energetic", "rockstar" or "native speaker" can put off qualified people. AI misses some phrases and can add its own bias, so you decide which changes to accept.

blocks.title: Tie every question to a requirement
blocks.body: Ask every candidate the same core questions, each linked to one listed requirement. For "manages competing deadlines", ask for a past situation and request a scoring guide for strong and weak answers. AI drafts, your team checks the questions are relevant and allowed under local employment rules.

blocks.question: Which prompt is the best start for a new job description?
options: Write a job ad for a great sales person.
Write a job ad for a sales coordinator. Daily duties: handle quotes, update the CRM. Must-have: 2 years of customer contact. Nice-to-have: CRM experience.
Copy our old ad and make it sound exciting.
blocks.explanation: Real duties and a clear split between must-haves and nice-to-haves give a focused, honest ad.
blocks.hint: Which prompt gives the assistant facts it cannot guess?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which phrases in a job ad deserve a bias check?
options: Young and energetic team
Native English speaker
Experience with budgeting
Uses CRM software daily
blocks.explanation: Age-coded and native-speaker wording can exclude qualified people. Skills and tools relate directly to the work.
blocks.hint: Which phrases describe a person rather than a skill?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt most effective.
blocks.prompt: Write 5 interview questions for a customer support role. ___ Give a short scoring guide for each.
options: Make them tough.
Tie each question to one requirement: handling upset customers, written clarity, teamwork.
Ask about family plans to see if they will stay.
blocks.explanation: Questions linked to listed requirements are fair and comparable. Personal-life questions are risky and unrelated to the job.
blocks.hint: Good questions point back to the job's requirements.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If AI reviews an ad for bias, you can publish it without reading again.
cards.explanation: AI misses things and can add bias. A person reads the final text.

cards.statement: Asking all candidates the same core questions makes comparison fairer.
cards.explanation: Consistency reduces the influence of first impressions.

cards.statement: Must-have lists should include every skill you would like.
cards.explanation: Only list what the job truly requires, or you shrink your pool.

blocks.hint: Think about who makes the final call.

blocks.question: AI suggests asking candidates how many children they have. What do you do?
options: Keep it, it helps plan schedules.
Remove it and keep only questions about job requirements.
Ask it only of candidates who seem to be parents.
blocks.explanation: Family questions are often restricted by local employment rules and invite bias. You are responsible for what you ask, not the tool.
blocks.hint: Does the question measure ability to do the job?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks your AI tool to draft a job ad or interview questions and to flag biased wording.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Using {{tool}}, write a prompt for a job description or a set of interview questions for a role on your team (pick one connected to this pain if you can). Include the real duties, must-haves, and a request to flag biased or exclusionary wording.
practice.default_context: You are an HR generalist who must hire a customer support agent and the old job ad is vague and full of buzzwords.

rubric.description: Gives real duties and separates must-have from nice-to-have skills.
Asks the AI to flag biased or exclusionary wording and suggest alternatives.
Asks for structured questions or content linked to listed requirements, with no personal data about real people.

practice.example_good_prompt: Draft a job ad for a customer support agent. Duties: answer tickets, escalate billing issues. Must-have: clear writing, 1 year of customer contact. Nice-to-have: helpdesk tool experience. Then review your draft for biased or exclusionary wording and suggest neutral alternatives. Finally write 5 structured interview questions, each tied to one must-have, with a scoring guide.

common_mistakes: Learners ask for "exciting" ads and get buzzwords. Steer them to real duties and must-haves.
Learners trust the bias check blindly. Remind them AI can miss wording and add its own bias.
Learners paste real employee details into prompts. Tell them to use roles, not names.
key_points: Describe the real job and separate must-haves from nice-to-haves.
AI flags biased wording, a person decides.
Same questions for every candidate, each tied to a requirement.
follow_up_tasks: Rewrite a sentence from an old job ad that sounds age- or culture-coded, then ask AI to review your version.

lessons.goal: Turn a policy into an FAQ or checklist with AI and verify it against the original.
lessons.title: Onboarding and policy materials

blocks.title: Handbook to FAQ
blocks.body: Paste one policy section and ask: "Write 6 FAQs for new hires. Use only this text. If the text does not answer a question, say 'not covered'." The last sentence matters: it stops the assistant from filling gaps with invented rules. Use a company-approved tool for internal documents.

blocks.title: Checklists and plain language
blocks.body: Ask for a first-week checklist by day, or a simpler version of a dense policy at a plain reading level. Add: "Keep all dates, amounts and obligations exactly as written." Simpler wording should never change the rule underneath it.

blocks.title: Check every answer
blocks.body: AI can soften a rule, drop an exception or invent a number. Compare each answer with the original: deadlines, eligibility, amounts, exceptions. Then ask the policy owner to approve it before sharing. An FAQ that sounds clear but is wrong creates more work than none.

blocks.question: Which instruction best keeps an AI-written FAQ accurate?
options: Write a friendly FAQ about our leave policy.
Write an FAQ using only the text below. If something is not covered, say 'not covered'.
Write an FAQ and add anything new hires usually wonder about.
blocks.explanation: Limiting the source and allowing "not covered" stops the assistant from inventing rules.
blocks.hint: Which prompt limits what the assistant may use?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What should you compare against the original policy?
options: Deadlines and notice periods
Who is eligible
How friendly the tone sounds
Exceptions and amounts
blocks.explanation: Details that change what employees must or may do are where simplified text goes wrong. Tone is a style choice.
blocks.hint: Focus on facts that affect people's actions.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt most effective.
blocks.prompt: Rewrite this expense policy in plain language for new hires. ___
options: Make it as short as you can.
Keep all limits, deadlines and approval steps exactly as written.
Remove anything complicated.
blocks.explanation: Plain language should change the wording only, not the rules.
blocks.hint: What must stay identical after simplification?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A clear, confident FAQ answer is probably correct.
cards.explanation: AI sounds confident even when it is wrong. Check against the source.

cards.statement: The policy owner should approve AI-written materials before they go out.
cards.explanation: The owner knows the exceptions and local rules.

cards.statement: Confidential internal documents can go into any free public chatbot.
cards.explanation: Use a company-approved tool and follow your data rules.

blocks.hint: Think about who is responsible for accuracy.

blocks.question: The AI's FAQ says employees get 10 days of notice, but you cannot find that number in the policy. What now?
options: Keep it, it sounds reasonable.
Delete or correct it using the original policy, and re-check the other answers.
Ask the AI to confirm and trust its reply.
blocks.explanation: An unsourced number is a likely invention, and the same tool may have invented others. Verify with the original.
blocks.hint: Which source is authoritative?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that turns a policy section into an FAQ or first-week checklist and keeps the answers faithful to the text.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Using {{tool}}, write a prompt that turns a policy section (assume you will paste it below your prompt) into a new-hire FAQ or checklist.
practice.default_context: You are an HR coordinator and new hires keep asking the same questions about remote work and vacation rules.

rubric.description: Tells the AI to use only the pasted text and to say when something is not covered.
Asks to keep dates, amounts and obligations unchanged.
Names the audience, format and length, such as 6 FAQs or a day-by-day checklist.

practice.example_good_prompt: Below is our remote work policy. Write 6 FAQs for new hires in plain language. Use only this text, and answer "not covered" when it does not say. Keep all dates, limits and approval steps exactly as written. Then list which sentences of the policy each answer relies on so I can check them.

common_mistakes: Learners skip the check because the FAQ reads well. Ask them to find each number in the original.
Learners allow the AI to "add common questions", which invites invented rules.
Learners paste confidential documents into unapproved tools.
key_points: Limit the AI to your text and allow "not covered".
Simpler wording must not change the rule.
Verify against the original and get owner approval.
follow_up_tasks: Take one AI-written FAQ answer and mark each fact with the policy sentence that supports it.

lessons.goal: Analyze anonymized survey comments with AI and keep every decision about people with humans.
lessons.title: Employee feedback and survey analysis

blocks.title: Remove personal data first
blocks.body: Before pasting comments into any AI tool, delete names, emails, job titles that identify one person, and team names for very small teams. Check that your tool is approved for employee data and follows local privacy rules. Anonymizing first is easier than undoing a leak.

blocks.title: Find themes, then actions
blocks.body: Ask: "Group these comments into themes with a rough count, add one anonymous quote each, and suggest two actions per theme." Treat counts as rough. Spot-check a sample of comments yourself, and look for important minority views the summary may flatten.

blocks.title: AI supports, people decide
blocks.body: AI can summarize feedback. It must not rank, score or screen employees or candidates on its own, or decide on pay, promotion or dismissal. Those decisions need a person who knows the context, can explain the reasoning, and follows local employment rules.

blocks.question: What do you do before pasting survey comments into an AI tool?
options: Paste them as they are, the tool will ignore names.
Remove names, emails and identifying details, and use a tool approved for employee data.
Keep names so the AI can group comments by person.
blocks.explanation: Personal data should be removed before sharing, and the tool should be approved by your organization.
blocks.hint: Think about what could identify a person.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which steps make AI theme analysis more reliable?
options: Asking for rough counts and one anonymous quote per theme
Reading a sample of raw comments yourself
Trusting the top three themes without checking
Looking for minority views the summary might miss
blocks.explanation: Samples, quotes and minority checks catch summaries that flatten or distort feedback.
blocks.hint: Which steps keep a human close to the data?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt most effective.
blocks.prompt: Here are 80 anonymized comments about workload. ___
options: Tell me who is unhappy.
Group them into themes with rough counts, one anonymous quote each, and two suggested actions per theme.
Summarize all of it in one sentence.
blocks.explanation: Themes, quotes and actions turn comments into something the team can discuss without exposing individuals.
blocks.hint: Aim for structure and no identification.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: AI can rank candidates and you can invite the top five without review.
cards.explanation: Automatic ranking can repeat hidden bias and may break local rules. People review every candidate.

cards.statement: AI can help summarize feedback that a manager then discusses with the team.
cards.explanation: Summaries support discussion, and people choose what to do.

cards.statement: If AI suggests a performance rating, HR can use it as the final rating.
cards.explanation: Decisions about people need human judgment and explanation.

blocks.hint: Who is accountable for decisions about people?

blocks.question: A manager asks AI to rank team members by how negative their feedback is. What is the best response?
options: Run it and share the ranking.
Decline, and use AI only to find themes in anonymized feedback.
Run it but hide the names.
blocks.explanation: Ranking people from feedback is a decision about people. AI can support analysis of themes, not judge individuals.
blocks.hint: Is this analysis or judgment of a person?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that analyzes anonymized survey comments for themes and actions, with no judgment about individuals.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Using {{tool}}, write a prompt for analyzing anonymized employee survey comments (assume they follow your prompt). Mention what you removed first.
practice.default_context: You are an HR business partner with 100 open-ended survey comments about workload and communication, and the leadership meeting is on Friday.

rubric.description: States that names and identifying details were removed and does not ask to identify anyone.
Requests themes, rough counts, anonymous quotes and suggested actions.
Asks for options to discuss and avoids ranking or judging individuals or teams.

practice.example_good_prompt: The comments below are anonymized, with names and identifying details removed. Group them into themes with rough counts and one anonymous quote each. For each theme suggest two actions for the leadership team to discuss. Flag views held by only a few people. Do not try to identify anyone and do not rank people or teams.

common_mistakes: Learners forget anonymizing and paste raw exports. Pause and ask what could identify someone.
Learners ask AI who is unhappy or which employee is weakest. Redirect to themes.
Learners accept counts as exact.
key_points: Remove personal data before using AI.
Ask for themes, quotes and suggested actions, then check a sample.
AI supports decisions about people and never makes them.
follow_up_tasks: Rewrite a prompt that asks for the "worst-performing" employee so it asks for themes instead.

courses.title: AI for Legal Professionals
courses.description: Use AI to summarize, compare and draft legal documents faster, while protecting client confidentiality and verifying every output.

lessons.goal: Decide what you may paste into an AI tool and anonymize a document before you prompt.
lessons.title: Confidentiality first

blocks.title: What stays out of the prompt
blocks.body: Depending on the tool, anything you paste may be stored, reviewed or used by the provider. Client names, privileged advice, case strategy and personal data are all covered by your confidentiality obligations. If you would not say it in a crowded lift, do not paste it into an unvetted tool.

blocks.title: Approved versus consumer tools
blocks.body: A **consumer** chatbot on a personal account is governed by terms you did not negotiate. A **firm-approved** tool has been reviewed, with contract terms on data use. Use only approved tools for client work. If unsure, ask IT or compliance before you paste.

blocks.title: Anonymize first
blocks.body: Replace identifying details with neutral labels. "Maria Keller owes Northwind Ltd 48,000 under the 2023 supply deal" becomes "Party A owes Party B an amount under a supply agreement." Remove names, account numbers and unusual facts that identify the matter. Keep a private key of your replacements.

blocks.question: You want AI to tighten a client's draft settlement offer. What is the safest first step?
options: Paste it into your personal chatbot, since you will check the result.
Use a firm-approved tool, or anonymize the text first if unsure.
Paste only the second half so the tool never sees everything.
Paste it into a free online editing tool.
blocks.explanation: The risk is where the data goes, not what you check afterwards. Approved tools and anonymization reduce it.
blocks.hint: Think about who controls the data once you press enter.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which items should you remove or replace before prompting an unvetted tool?
options: The client's name
A generic request such as 'make this clause shorter'
Bank account numbers
A rare detail that would let anyone identify the matter
blocks.explanation: Names, account numbers and distinctive facts can identify the client. A generic editing request does not.
blocks.hint: Ask whether a stranger could work out who the matter is about.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that anonymizes this prompt properly.
blocks.prompt: Summarize the dispute between ___ over late delivery under the supply agreement.
options: Maria Keller and Northwind Ltd
M. Keller and Northwind
Party A and Party B
blocks.explanation: Initials and shortened names still identify people. Neutral labels do not.
blocks.hint: Which option could a stranger not trace back to a person?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A tool being free and popular means it is safe for client matters.
cards.explanation: Popularity says nothing about data terms.

cards.statement: Replacing the client's name with a label is enough if unusual facts stay in.
cards.explanation: Distinctive facts can still identify the matter.

cards.statement: If you are unsure whether a tool is approved, you should ask before pasting.
cards.explanation: You cannot undo a paste, so check first.

blocks.hint: You cannot take a paste back.

blocks.question: Your firm has no approved tool yet and you must summarize a privileged memo. What do you do?
options: Use a consumer tool with chat history off.
Summarize it manually or ask compliance.
Paste it with the names removed only.
Split it into five parts and paste each separately.
blocks.explanation: Privileged content needs an approved channel. Settings or splitting the text do not fix the exposure.
blocks.hint: Ask whether any option actually fixes where the text goes.

practice.instructions: Rewrite a short, realistic work scenario as an anonymized prompt you could safely send to an AI tool.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Describe a realistic example of that task in 3-4 sentences, then rewrite it as a prompt for {{tool}} with all identifying details replaced by neutral labels. Add one sentence saying which details you removed and why.
practice.default_context: A lawyer must ask AI to simplify a paragraph from a client's employment dispute letter that names the client, the employer and a salary figure.

rubric.description: Names, places, numbers and unusual facts are replaced by neutral labels.
The anonymized prompt still contains enough context for a useful answer.
States which details were removed and links them to confidentiality obligations.

practice.example_good_prompt: Simplify this paragraph for a non-lawyer. Employee A claims Employer B ended the contract without the notice the agreement requires. Keep a neutral tone and a maximum of 80 words. (Removed: names, salary, dates and the employer's industry, because they could identify the client.)

common_mistakes: Learners think removing only the name is enough. Show how dates, amounts and unusual facts still identify a matter.
Learners treat settings such as chat history as a substitute for approval. Steer them to approved tools and compliance.
key_points: Your confidentiality obligations apply to every tool you paste into.
Use approved tools for client work and anonymize when unsure.
Keep a private key so you can restore details afterwards.
follow_up_tasks: Take a paragraph from a past matter and list every detail that could identify the client.

lessons.goal: Get a structured summary or comparison from AI and check each point against the source text.
lessons.title: Summarizing and comparing documents

blocks.title: Summaries with structure
blocks.body: Do not ask "summarize this contract". Say who the summary is for and what to cover: parties, term, payment, termination, liability and unusual clauses. Ask for a table or bullet list.

blocks.title: Compare two versions
blocks.body: Give the tool both versions, anonymized, and ask for a table of every change: clause number, old wording, new wording, and who it favors. Ask it to flag small changes that alter meaning, such as "may" replaced by "shall". Then read those clauses yourself.

blocks.title: Make it quote its sources
blocks.body: AI can misread a clause or describe one that is not there. Add: "For each point, quote the exact sentence you rely on and give the clause number." A missing or mismatched quote is your warning.

blocks.question: Which prompt is most likely to give you a useful contract summary?
options: Summarize this contract.
Summarize this anonymized services agreement for a partner. Cover term, payment, termination and liability in a table.
Tell me if this contract is good.
Rewrite this contract in simpler words.
blocks.explanation: Audience, topics and format give the tool clear boundaries. Asking whether a contract is good asks for a judgment that is yours.
blocks.hint: Look for the prompt that names the audience and the sections.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt easiest to verify.
blocks.prompt: List the main termination rights in the attached agreement. ___
options: Be brief.
For each right, quote the exact sentence and give the clause number.
Only include the important ones.
blocks.explanation: Quotes and clause numbers let you spot invented or misread text.
blocks.hint: What would let you check each point in seconds?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What should a good comparison of two contract versions include?
options: Clause number for each change
Old and new wording side by side
A verdict that the new version is safe to sign
A flag for small changes that could alter meaning
blocks.explanation: Locating changes and exposing subtle shifts supports your review. Whether to sign is your judgment.
blocks.hint: Ask which option replaces your review with the tool's verdict.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If an AI summary sounds confident, you can skip reading the clauses it cites.
cards.explanation: Confidence is not accuracy. Always check the cited clause.

cards.statement: A quote that cannot be found in the document is a sign the AI may have invented it.
cards.explanation: Search the original for the quoted words. If they are missing, do not rely on that point.

cards.statement: An issue-spotting list from AI replaces your own review.
cards.explanation: It points you to clauses, but you read and judge them.

blocks.hint: Ask who is responsible for the final review.

blocks.question: The AI says the notice period is 30 days, but its quote is not in the contract. What do you do?
options: Trust the summary, since the rest matched.
Search the contract yourself, correct the point and check the others.
Ask again and use the better-sounding answer.
Delete the notice period from your notes.
blocks.explanation: A false quote shows the tool can be wrong, so check the source and review the other points.
blocks.hint: One error lowers your trust in the other points.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks AI to summarize or compare a document and forces it to quote its sources.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} asking for an anonymized document summary or comparison. Say who it is for, which points to cover, the output format, and how the tool must show the source text for each point.
practice.default_context: A paralegal must compare two versions of an anonymized supply agreement and tell the supervising lawyer which clauses changed.

rubric.description: Names who the summary is for and which clauses or topics to cover.
Asks for a table, list or other structure.
Asks for exact quotes and clause numbers for every point.

practice.example_good_prompt: Compare the two anonymized versions of this supply agreement for a supervising lawyer. Give a table with clause number, old wording, new wording and who it favors. Flag small wording changes that alter meaning. For each row, quote the exact sentence from each version. Do not say whether to sign.

common_mistakes: Learners ask whether a contract is good or safe. Redirect them to ask for facts and clause locations, not conclusions.
Learners read only the summary. Have them open two cited clauses and compare.
key_points: Name the audience, topics and format.
Ask for exact quotes and clause numbers on every point.
AI points you to clauses; you read them and decide.
follow_up_tasks: Ask AI to summarize a short anonymized clause and check every quote against the original.

lessons.goal: Produce a first draft with AI and check every legal statement and citation before it goes out.
lessons.title: Drafting first versions

blocks.title: Good first drafts
blocks.body: AI is fast at letters, standard clauses and checklists. Give it the purpose, reader, tone, facts and length. Mark gaps with "[to confirm]" rather than letting it guess. You get a structure to edit, not a finished document.

blocks.title: Invented authorities
blocks.body: AI can invent case names, citations, quotations and legal rules that look completely real. Look up every authority in a trusted source, open it, and confirm it says what the draft claims. If you cannot find it, delete it.

blocks.title: You decide and sign
blocks.body: AI output is not legal advice. It does not know your jurisdiction, your client's goals or recent changes in the law. You review, correct and take responsibility for what goes out under your name. Ask the tool to list its assumptions, then check them.

blocks.question: Which request is best for a first-draft letter?
options: Write a demand letter.
Draft a polite but firm payment reminder to Party B, 150 words, citing the invoice due date. Mark missing facts as [to confirm].
Write a letter that will win.
Write whatever you think the law requires.
blocks.explanation: Purpose, reader, tone, length and a rule for gaps produce an editable draft. The other requests invite guesses.
blocks.hint: Look for purpose, tone, length and missing-facts handling.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: AI can produce a convincing case citation for a case that does not exist.
cards.explanation: The tool generates plausible text, not verified sources.

cards.statement: If a citation is formatted correctly, it is probably real.
cards.explanation: Formatting says nothing about existence. Look it up in a trusted source.

cards.statement: You should open each cited authority and check that it supports the statement.
cards.explanation: A real case can be cited for something it does not say.

blocks.hint: Plausible does not mean real.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Before a draft with legal references goes to a client, you should:
options: Look up each authority in a trusted source
Confirm each authority says what the draft claims
Keep any citation the AI repeats when asked if it is sure
Delete anything you cannot verify
blocks.explanation: Verification means finding and reading the source. Asking the AI is not verification.
blocks.hint: The tool cannot check its own work reliably.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this drafting prompt safest.
blocks.prompt: Draft a first-version confidentiality clause for an anonymized services agreement. ___
options: Add case law to support it.
Use standard wording, list your assumptions, and cite no cases or statutes.
Make it as strong as possible.
blocks.explanation: Assumptions give you something to check, and banning citations removes the risk of invented authorities.
blocks.hint: Which option reduces what you must verify?

blocks.question: A colleague says, "The AI wrote it, so it is the tool's advice, not mine." Best response?
options: Correct, as long as you note the tool was used.
The lawyer who signs is responsible, so you must review and own every word.
Correct for routine letters only.
Only the legal citations are your responsibility.
blocks.explanation: AI output is never legal advice. The signing lawyer is responsible for the whole document.
blocks.hint: Who signs the letter?

practice.instructions: Write a drafting prompt that gets a usable first version and builds in verification.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} to draft a first version of a letter, clause or checklist for that task. Give purpose, reader, tone, length and anonymized facts, mark unknowns, and tell the tool how to handle citations and assumptions.
practice.default_context: A legal assistant must draft a first-version reminder letter to a supplier who missed a delivery date, for a lawyer to review and sign.

rubric.description: States purpose, reader, tone and length, using anonymized facts.
Marks unknown facts for confirmation instead of letting the tool guess.
Forbids invented citations or asks for assumptions to review, and notes that a lawyer will verify and sign.

practice.example_good_prompt: Draft a first-version letter from Party A to Party B reminding them of a missed delivery date under a supply agreement. Polite but firm, 150 words. Use [to confirm] for any missing dates or amounts. Do not cite cases or statutes. List your assumptions at the end. A lawyer will review and sign.

common_mistakes: Learners ask AI to add case law to strengthen a draft. Explain that invented authorities are the biggest risk and show how to ban citations.
Learners treat the draft as final. Remind them that the signing lawyer owns every word.
key_points: Give purpose, reader, tone and length, and mark unknown facts.
Verify every citation and legal statement in a trusted source.
AI output is never legal advice; the lawyer decides and signs.
follow_up_tasks: Ask AI for a short clause with assumptions listed, then verify each assumption against your own knowledge or sources.

courses.title: AI for Marketers
courses.description: Write briefs that produce testable copy, turn real customer feedback into themes, and turn campaign exports into next tests, while checking what the AI tells you.

lessons.goal: Write a short brief with voice, audience and channel, and ask for several variants to test.
lessons.title: Briefs and copy variations

blocks.title: Brief it like a freelancer
blocks.body: AI does not know your brand. Give it what you would give a new freelancer: who the audience is, the channel, the goal, your tone, and one sample of copy you like. Add words to avoid. Without this, you get generic text that fits any company.

blocks.title: Ask for variants, not one perfect text
blocks.body: Nobody can predict the winner. Ask for five subject lines, each with a different angle: price, urgency, curiosity, social proof, a plain benefit. Then pick two and A/B test them.

blocks.title: Cut the AI sound
blocks.body: Generic phrases like "elevate your journey" give the AI away. Say "no buzzwords, short sentences, mention one concrete detail". Then edit the draft yourself and check every claim, such as discounts and dates.

blocks.question: You need a newsletter subject line for a spring sale. Which request works best?
options: Write a great subject line for our sale.
Write 5 subject lines for our spring sale email to existing customers. Friendly tone, under 45 characters, each with a different angle.
Write the best possible subject line, make it viral.
blocks.explanation: It names the audience, channel, tone and length, and asks for several angles you can test.
blocks.hint: Which request leaves the AI the least to guess?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which details belong in a copy brief?
options: Who the audience is
Words and claims to avoid
Your private customer email list
A sample of copy in your brand voice
blocks.explanation: Audience, limits and a voice sample shape the output. Customer lists are personal data and never belong in a public tool.
blocks.hint: Think about what is safe to paste into a public tool.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt most useful for testing.
blocks.prompt: Write ad headlines for our meal-kit trial offer. ___ Keep each under 30 characters.
options: Make them all perfect.
Give me 6, each using a different angle: price, speed, taste, convenience, guarantee, curiosity.
Write one in the style of a famous brand.
blocks.explanation: Distinct angles give you real differences to test, not six rewrites of the same idea.
blocks.hint: A test needs options that differ from each other.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: AI may invent a discount or a feature your product does not have.
cards.explanation: It writes what sounds likely, so check every claim against your offer.

cards.statement: A single polished AI draft is better than several variants.
cards.explanation: Variants let real audiences pick the winner instead of your guess.

cards.statement: A sample of your past copy helps match your brand voice.
cards.explanation: AI copies examples well, which is faster than describing a tone in adjectives.

blocks.hint: Think about who decides what works, you or your audience.

blocks.question: The draft says "Elevate your journey with our innovative solution." What is the best next prompt?
options: Make it more exciting.
Rewrite it with no buzzwords, short sentences, and one concrete benefit: setup takes 10 minutes.
Make it longer.
blocks.explanation: Banning buzzwords and requiring a concrete detail removes the generic tone.
blocks.hint: Vague feedback gets vague rewrites.

practice.instructions: Write a brief that asks your AI tool for several copy variants for one real channel. Include audience, tone and limits.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that asks for 4 to 5 copy variants for one channel related to this pain. Include the audience, the channel, the tone, words to avoid, and what makes each variant different.
practice.default_context: You are a marketing manager at a small online shop. You need subject lines for a weekend sale email to existing customers.

rubric.description: Names the audience, the channel and the goal of the copy.
Requests several versions with different angles, not one.
States tone, length and words or claims to avoid.

practice.example_good_prompt: Write 5 subject lines for a weekend sale email to existing customers of a small pet shop. Friendly, plain tone, under 45 characters, no exclamation marks or buzzwords. Each one uses a different angle (price, urgency, curiosity, social proof, benefit). Only mention the 20% discount that ends Sunday.

common_mistakes: Asking for one perfect text. Steer toward several variants with different angles.
Leaving out the audience and channel. Ask who will read it and where.
Pasting customer names or emails into the prompt. Remind them to use anonymous descriptions.
key_points: A brief has audience, channel, goal, tone and limits.
Variants with different angles are testable.
You check claims and edit before publishing.
follow_up_tasks: Rewrite a weak one-line prompt into a full brief for a LinkedIn post.
Take one AI draft and list every claim that needs checking.

lessons.goal: Turn customer reviews or survey answers into themes and personas, and check them against the source.
lessons.title: Audience research from real data

blocks.title: Use your data, not its imagination
blocks.body: Ask AI to invent your customer and you get a stereotype. Instead, paste real material: reviews, survey answers, support tickets. Say "use only the text below". Now it summarizes your customers rather than guessing about them.

blocks.title: Themes with evidence
blocks.body: Ask for the top themes, how many comments mention each, and two short quotes per theme. Quotes let you check the source. Example: 40 reviews of a running shoe might show "runs small" and "great for wide feet".

blocks.title: Clean data first
blocks.body: Remove names, emails and order numbers before pasting into a public tool. Then spot-check: search your data for a quote and count a theme yourself. Treat personas as a hypothesis to test, not a fact.

blocks.question: You want a persona for your yoga app. What is the most reliable approach?
options: Ask: describe our typical customer.
Paste 50 anonymized survey answers and ask for a persona using only that text, with quotes.
Ask for the persona of the average yoga fan in your country.
blocks.explanation: Grounding the answer in your own data keeps the persona tied to real customers.
blocks.hint: Where does the information about your customers actually live?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What should you ask for to make themes easy to check?
options: A count of comments for each theme
Two short quotes per theme
A short summary that leaves out the details
A note on comments that fit no theme
blocks.explanation: Counts, quotes and leftovers let you verify the summary and spot what it ignored. A summary without details cannot be checked.
blocks.hint: Pick what lets you go back to the source.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that keeps the AI honest.
blocks.prompt: Below are 60 customer reviews. Find the 5 most common complaints. ___ Reviews: ...
options: Fill any gaps with what customers usually say.
Use only these reviews, quote one for each complaint, and say if there is too little evidence.
Write the complaints in a positive, persuasive tone.
blocks.explanation: Restricting it to the text and asking for quotes reduces invented findings.
blocks.hint: You want the answer limited to what is on the page.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: It is fine to paste a spreadsheet with customer names and emails into a public AI tool.
cards.explanation: Remove personal data first, or use a tool your company has approved.

cards.statement: A theme the AI reports should be spot-checked against the source.
cards.explanation: Search for a quote and count a few mentions yourself.

cards.statement: A persona from 10 survey answers proves what all customers want.
cards.explanation: A small sample gives a hypothesis. Test it with more data.

blocks.hint: Ask yourself how you would prove each claim to your boss.

blocks.question: The AI says "most customers love the packaging", but you see only a few mentions in the reviews. What do you do?
options: Keep it. The AI read all the reviews.
Ask it for the exact quotes and the count, then fix the claim to match.
Delete the theme and ask for a new one.
blocks.explanation: Asking for evidence shows whether the claim holds, and you correct it to match the data.
blocks.hint: Evidence first, then decide.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks AI to find themes in customer feedback, using only the data you provide and showing evidence.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that analyzes a set of customer feedback (reviews, survey answers or tickets) related to this pain. Say what data you will paste, what to produce, and how the AI should show evidence.
practice.default_context: You are a marketing specialist at a software company. You have 80 anonymized support tickets and want the top reasons new users get stuck.

rubric.description: Tells the AI to use only the pasted feedback and not invent customers.
Requests counts or quotes for each theme.
Mentions removing names, emails or other personal data first.

practice.example_good_prompt: Below are 80 support tickets from new users with names and emails removed. Use only this text. Find the top 5 reasons users get stuck during setup. For each, give the number of tickets, two short quotes, and one question we could ask in a survey. List tickets that fit no theme. If evidence is thin, say so.

common_mistakes: Asking for a persona with no data. Ask what real material they can paste.
Accepting themes without counts or quotes. Have them request evidence.
Pasting raw data with names or emails. Show how to anonymize first.
key_points: AI summarizes your data. It does not know your customers.
Quotes and counts make themes checkable.
Personas are hypotheses until tested.
follow_up_tasks: Take five reviews, ask for themes with quotes, and verify each quote exists.
Rewrite "describe our customer" as a data-grounded prompt.

lessons.goal: Turn a metrics export into insights and next tests, and double-check the numbers the AI quotes.
lessons.title: Campaign reporting

blocks.title: Give context with the numbers
blocks.body: A raw export tells AI little. Add the goal, the period and what changed, such as a new landing page. Ask: "What stands out, and what might explain it?" Context turns a list of numbers into a useful read.

blocks.title: Ask for hypotheses and tests
blocks.body: A description repeats the table. Ask instead: "Give 3 hypotheses for why email B had lower clicks, and one test for each." Example: a hypothesis about an unclear button leads to a test of two button labels.

blocks.title: Recheck every number
blocks.body: AI can miscalculate, mix up columns or round badly. Recompute any figure you will present: totals, rates, changes. Remove customer data before pasting. Remember, an insight is a lead to test, not proof of cause.

blocks.question: Your paid social export shows clicks fell 20% last week. Which prompt gets the most useful answer?
options: Summarize this data.
Goal: lead signups. Last week we changed the ad image. Suggest 3 hypotheses for the click drop and one test for each.
Tell me why the campaign failed.
blocks.explanation: It gives context and asks for explanations you can test, not a description.
blocks.hint: Which prompt gives the AI more than the numbers to work with?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which numbers should you recompute before they go into a report?
options: A conversion rate the AI calculated
A percent change between two weeks
A total spend figure in the summary
A general sentence like "email is a useful channel"
blocks.explanation: Calculated figures can be wrong. Recompute any number your readers will rely on.
blocks.hint: Look for figures with a calculation behind them.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that turns a summary into a plan.
blocks.prompt: Here is our email report for March. ___ Keep it to one paragraph and a table.
options: Describe every row.
Suggest 3 hypotheses for the low open rate on Tuesday sends and a test for each.
Say whether it was good or bad.
blocks.explanation: Hypotheses with tests give you next actions, not just a recap.
blocks.hint: You want ideas you can act on.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If the AI explains why a metric dropped, you can treat it as the proven cause.
cards.explanation: Its explanation is a hypothesis. Only a test can confirm a cause.

cards.statement: AI can make arithmetic mistakes on a spreadsheet export.
cards.explanation: Recompute key numbers in your spreadsheet before sharing them.

cards.statement: Adding the campaign goal makes the analysis more relevant.
cards.explanation: The goal tells it which metrics matter most.

blocks.hint: Separate what the data shows from what explains it.

blocks.question: The AI says your newsletter click rate was 4.8%, but your platform shows 3.9%. What now?
options: Use the AI figure. It looked at all the data.
Trust the platform, then ask the AI to show how it calculated 4.8% to find the mismatch.
Average the two numbers.
blocks.explanation: Your platform is the source. Asking for the calculation reveals the cause, such as a wrong denominator or a different definition of a click.
blocks.hint: Which number comes from the original source?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that gives AI a metrics export with context and asks for hypotheses and next tests, not just a summary.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that analyzes a campaign metrics export related to this pain. Include the goal, the period, what changed, and ask for hypotheses, tests and a way to double-check the numbers.
practice.default_context: You are a marketing manager. Last month's email campaign had a lower click rate than the month before, and you must report to your director on Friday.

rubric.description: States the goal, the period and what changed.
Requests explanations and next experiments, not only a description.
Asks for calculations to be shown or says you will recheck key numbers.

practice.example_good_prompt: The goal is more demo requests from email. Below is the export for March and April, with no subscriber data. In April we shortened the subject lines. Give 3 hypotheses for the lower click rate, one test for each, and the metrics I should watch. Show how you calculated each rate so I can check it.

common_mistakes: Asking only for a summary. Push them to ask for hypotheses and tests.
Trusting calculated figures. Have them recompute one number in a spreadsheet.
Treating a hypothesis as the cause. Remind them to run a test.
key_points: Give goal, period and changes with the data.
Ask for hypotheses and a test for each.
Recheck every number before sharing.
follow_up_tasks: Take a small export and compare the AI's rate with your own calculation.
Turn one hypothesis into an A/B test with a clear success metric.

courses.title: AI for Small Business Owners
courses.description: Use an AI assistant to answer customers, plan marketing and make sense of your sales numbers, while checking every result yourself.

lessons.goal: Draft customer replies and an FAQ with AI that sound like you and promise only what you can deliver.
lessons.title: Answer customers fast, in your own voice

blocks.title: Give the facts, get a draft
blocks.body: AI writes a good reply when you hand it the facts. Paste the customer's message, say what happened and name what you can offer. Example: a cake arrived late. Tell the AI "we were 40 minutes late, I can refund the delivery fee." Ask for a short, warm reply. Remove names and phone numbers first.

blocks.title: Keep your own voice
blocks.body: Paste two or three of your past replies and say "write like this." Add rules: "friendly, no corporate phrases, first name only." For a negative review, ask for a calm reply that thanks the person, owns the real problem and offers to talk offline.

blocks.title: You own every promise
blocks.body: AI tends to agree and please, so it may invent refunds, deadlines or policies. Before sending, read the draft for anything you have not agreed to. Delete it or fix it. Then turn your repeated questions into an FAQ: paste ten real questions and your true answers, and ask for a tidy list.

blocks.question: A customer complains that her order arrived damaged. What do you give the AI to get a useful reply?
options: Only the complaint, and ask it to fix things.
The complaint, what happened, and what you are willing to offer.
A request for the most generous reply possible.
blocks.explanation: The AI cannot know what you will offer. Facts and limits let it draft something you can send.
blocks.hint: Think about what the AI cannot know about your shop.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If the AI writes "full refund within 24 hours," it is safe to send as is.
cards.explanation: The AI invents policies. Only send what you have decided.

cards.statement: A draft reply should be read before it goes out.
cards.explanation: You are responsible for every word that carries your business name.

cards.statement: You can paste a customer's full name and address into any AI tool.
cards.explanation: Remove personal details first. Write "the customer" instead.

blocks.hint: Who is responsible once the message is sent?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that keeps the reply sounding like you.
blocks.prompt: Reply to this review. ___ Thank the guest and offer to talk by phone.
options: Be professional.
Here are two of my past replies. Match their warm, casual tone.
Sound like a big company.
