blocks.explanation: Real examples teach tone better than a single word like professional.
blocks.hint: Show, do not just tell.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which steps help with a negative review?
options: Ask for a calm tone that owns the real problem.
Let the AI argue that the customer is wrong.
Offer to continue the conversation privately.
Include the reviewer's order details in your prompt.
blocks.explanation: A calm, honest reply that moves offline protects your reputation. Arguing and sharing details do not.
blocks.hint: Picture a future customer reading your public reply.

blocks.question: You want an FAQ page. What is the best input?
options: Ask AI to guess common questions.
Ten real customer questions plus your true answers.
Your competitor's FAQ, copied.
blocks.explanation: Real questions and your true answers make an FAQ that is accurate for your business.
blocks.hint: Where do your true answers live?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that gets a draft reply to a difficult customer message, in your voice and without invented promises.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Using {{tool}}, write a prompt that drafts a reply to an unhappy customer message related to this. Include the facts, what you can offer, your tone, and what the AI must not promise.
practice.default_context: You run a small cafe. A customer says her birthday cake order was 40 minutes late and wants her money back. You can refund the delivery fee only.

rubric.description: States what happened and the customer's message, without personal data.
Names what can be offered and tells the AI not to promise anything else.
Asks for a specific tone or includes a sample of the owner's writing.

practice.example_good_prompt: Reply to this customer message (name removed). Facts: our cake arrived 40 minutes late. I can refund the delivery fee only, nothing more. Tone: warm, plain, like my past replies below. Do not promise a full refund or a free order. Keep it under 80 words.

common_mistakes: Learners paste the full complaint with names; remind them to anonymize first.
Learners send the draft unread; have them mark every promise in it.
key_points: Give facts and limits, the AI supplies wording.
Examples of your past replies carry your voice.
You are responsible for every promise.
follow_up_tasks: Take a real review and write a prompt with three facts and one thing the AI must not promise.

lessons.goal: Create social posts, product descriptions and a one-week content plan that fit your local customers and make only true claims.
lessons.title: Marketing on a budget

blocks.title: Say who you are talking to
blocks.body: "Write a post for my bakery" gives a generic result. Add your town, your customers and the offer. Example: "Post for parents near Elm Street. Friday only, buy two croissants, get a third. Friendly, two sentences." Ask for three versions and pick the one that sounds like you.

blocks.title: Describe real products
blocks.body: Give the AI your facts: materials, size, what makes the item different. Ask for a short description for a shop page. Then check each claim. If the AI writes "organic" or "handmade in small batches" and it is not true, remove it.

blocks.title: Plan one week at a time
blocks.body: Tell the AI your days open, your slowest day and one goal. Ask for a table: day, post idea, photo to take. Then do the work in batches. A plan you can finish beats a perfect plan you skip.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this post request work best.
blocks.prompt: Write an Instagram post for my hair salon. ___ Two sentences, friendly tone.
options: Make it go viral.
Our customers are locals in a small town. Offer: 15 percent off cuts on Tuesdays, our slowest day.
Use lots of trendy words.
blocks.explanation: Audience, place and a concrete offer turn a generic post into one that fits your business.
blocks.hint: What does the AI not know about your customers?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: AI can add features to a product description that you did not give it.
cards.explanation: It may invent materials or claims, so check every detail.

cards.statement: Asking for three versions of a post helps you pick your best one.
cards.explanation: Comparing options is faster than rewriting one draft.

cards.statement: A content plan should include as many posts per day as possible.
cards.explanation: A plan you can actually keep is more useful than a big one.

blocks.hint: Think about who verifies the facts.

blocks.question: What should you tell the AI to get a useful weekly plan?
options: Just: make me a plan.
Your open days, slowest day, one goal and how much time you have.
Your yearly revenue.
blocks.explanation: Real constraints make the plan something you can follow.
blocks.hint: A plan has to fit your week.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which details make a post feel local?
options: A nearby street or neighborhood name.
A seasonal event in your town.
Generic phrases like best quality ever.
A limited offer for your quietest day.
blocks.explanation: Local details and specific offers feel real. Generic phrases could belong to anyone.
blocks.hint: Which details could only come from your business?

blocks.question: The AI describes your candles as "100 percent natural." You have not confirmed this. What do you do?
options: Post it, it sounds great.
Remove or confirm the claim before posting.
Ask the AI if it is sure.
blocks.explanation: The AI cannot verify your product. You must confirm claims before customers rely on them.
blocks.hint: Who actually knows what is in the candles?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that creates a week of social content for your business, tailored to local customers.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Using {{tool}}, write a prompt for a one-week content plan that helps with this. Include your customers, your location, one offer, and the format you want.
practice.default_context: You own a small flower shop in a neighborhood with many young families. Tuesdays are slow. You can post three times a week.

rubric.description: Names who the customers are and where they are.
States posting days, time or the slow day and one offer.
Asks for a table or list with post ideas and the photo to take.

practice.example_good_prompt: I own a flower shop in a neighborhood with many young families. Tuesdays are slow. Make a one-week plan with three posts as a table - day, post idea, photo to take. Include a Tuesday offer of 10 percent off bouquets. Friendly, short, no invented facts about our flowers.

common_mistakes: Prompts that skip location and offer, producing generic posts.
Learners keep AI product claims they cannot confirm.
key_points: Audience, place and offer make a post local.
Check every product claim.
Plan only what you can finish.
follow_up_tasks: Rewrite a generic post prompt to include a street name, an offer and a tone.

lessons.goal: Use AI to clean a sales export, compare supplier prices and spot trends, then check the totals yourself.
lessons.title: Make sense of your numbers

blocks.title: Clean the mess
blocks.body: Sales exports often have mixed date formats, duplicate rows and inconsistent product names. Paste a few sample rows, remove customer names, and ask the AI how to fix them in your spreadsheet. Ask for the formula or steps, not just the result, so you can repeat it next month.

blocks.title: Compare and spot trends
blocks.body: Give the AI supplier prices for the same items and ask for a side-by-side table. Or paste monthly sales and ask "what changed?" It can point out that Saturdays are your best day. Use it to organize and explain, not to decide prices or taxes.

blocks.title: Check the totals yourself
blocks.body: AI can make arithmetic errors and miss rows. Compare its totals with your spreadsheet's SUM. Spot check two or three numbers by hand. For taxes, pricing decisions or loans, ask your accountant.

blocks.question: Your sales export has dates in three different formats. What is the best prompt?
options: Fix my data.
Here are five sample rows. Explain how to convert all dates to one format in my spreadsheet.
Here is my whole customer list, clean it.
blocks.explanation: Sample rows and a request for steps keeps data private and gives you a method you can reuse.
blocks.hint: You want a method, not just a one-time fix.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: AI totals are always correct because computers are good at math.
cards.explanation: AI assistants can make arithmetic errors, so compare with a spreadsheet SUM.

cards.statement: Asking AI which supplier is cheapest for each item is a good use.
cards.explanation: Side-by-side comparison is organizing data. Still check the table against your price lists.

cards.statement: AI can tell you exactly how much tax you owe.
cards.explanation: Tax decisions need your accountant and official rules.

blocks.hint: Who is responsible for your numbers?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this request safe and useful.
blocks.prompt: Here are 10 sample rows from my sales export. ___ Tell me how to remove duplicates.
options: I removed customer names and emails.
The rows are real, so I kept customer names and emails to stay accurate.
Please guess any values that are missing.
blocks.explanation: Remove personal details before pasting data into a public AI tool.
blocks.hint: What should never leave your shop in a prompt?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. How do you check AI output on your numbers?
options: Compare its total with the spreadsheet SUM.
Recalculate two or three rows by hand.
Trust it if it sounds confident.
Look for rows it may have skipped.
blocks.explanation: Confident tone proves nothing. Totals, spot checks and row counts catch mistakes.
blocks.hint: Which checks use your own data?

blocks.question: The AI says you should raise prices by 12 percent to improve profit. What is the right response?
options: Raise prices right away.
Treat it as an idea, check your costs and customers, and ask your accountant if unsure.
Ask the AI to confirm, and raise prices if it agrees.
blocks.explanation: AI does not see your full costs or market. Decisions about money remain yours.
blocks.hint: Does the AI know your whole business?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks AI to organize or compare your numbers and tells it how you will verify the result.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Using {{tool}}, write a prompt that helps you organize numbers related to this. Describe the data, what you want back, and how you will check it. Do not include personal data.
practice.default_context: You run an online store. Your monthly sales export has duplicate rows and dates in two formats, and you also have prices from two suppliers for the same ten items.

rubric.description: Explains the columns or gives sample rows without customer personal data.
Asks for steps, a formula or a table, such as a side-by-side price comparison.
Says the owner will check totals, and asks for no financial or tax advice.

practice.example_good_prompt: My sales export has columns date, product, quantity, price. Dates come in two formats and some rows are duplicated. Here are 5 sample rows with no customer data. Explain how to clean this in a spreadsheet and give a formula for the total. I will check the total with SUM. Do not give financial advice.

common_mistakes: Pasting customer lists with personal data; steer toward sample rows.
Accepting AI totals without a check.
key_points: Ask for steps and formulas you can reuse.
Remove personal data first.
AI organizes and explains; you verify, and an accountant advises.
follow_up_tasks: Take ten rows of sales and compare the AI's total with your own SUM.

courses.title: AI for Teachers
courses.description: Use an AI assistant to draft differentiated lesson plans, quizzes, rubrics and feedback comments faster, while keeping student data private and every decision in your hands.

lessons.goal: Write a prompt that produces a usable lesson activity in three difficulty levels, then adapt it to your class.
lessons.title: Lesson plans that fit every level

blocks.title: Give the full picture
blocks.body:
AI does not know your class, so "Make a fractions lesson" returns a generic plan. Tell it the goal, grade, time, materials and anything special about the group.

Example: "Grade 5 math, 45 minutes, goal: add fractions with unlike denominators, no printer, 4 students read below level."

blocks.title: Ask for versions
blocks.body:
Ask for the same task at three levels: support, core and extension. Keep the learning goal identical, so every student works toward the same target.

You can also ask for sentence starters or a shorter reading text.

blocks.title: You adapt, AI drafts
blocks.body: Treat the output as a first draft. Check the timing, the content and whether the tasks suit your students. Ask for changes in a follow-up message instead of starting over.

blocks.question: Which prompt will give you the most usable lesson draft?
options: Plan a good lesson about the water cycle.
Grade 4 science, 40 minutes, goal: explain evaporation and condensation. 26 students, 3 new English learners. One hands-on activity.
Plan a fun science lesson for children.
blocks.explanation: Goal, level, time and class needs let the AI tailor the draft instead of guessing.
blocks.hint: Look for the prompt that tells the AI about your actual classroom.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which details belong in a differentiation prompt?
options: The learning goal all students must reach
Names and grades of individual students
How many levels you want, such as support, core and extension
What kind of support the lower level needs, such as sentence starters
blocks.explanation: The goal, the levels and the type of support shape the versions. Student names add privacy risk and no value.
blocks.hint: Ask which detail the AI does not need to build the versions.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that completes the prompt best.
blocks.prompt: Create a 20-minute group activity on persuasive writing for Grade 8. ___
options: Make it easy for some students and hard for others.
Give three versions, support, core and extension, with one goal: students support a claim with evidence.
Change the task for every student.
blocks.explanation: Three named levels with one shared goal keep the versions comparable and the target fair.
blocks.hint: Good versions change the support, not the target.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A plan from AI is ready to teach without changes.
cards.explanation: You know your students and your time. Always review and adjust.

cards.statement: If the first draft misses the mark, you can ask for changes in a follow-up message.
cards.explanation: Follow-ups are the fastest way to refine a draft.

cards.statement: AI can suggest an activity that takes more time than you have.
cards.explanation: Timing is a common weak spot, so check it against your period.

blocks.hint: Think about who knows your class best.

blocks.question: The support version of an AI activity is far too easy. What do you do?
options: Use it as it is, since the AI wrote it for that level.
Ask the AI to raise the difficulty slightly, keep the sentence starters, then review it.
Delete everything and write the whole plan alone.
blocks.explanation: A targeted follow-up fixes the gap quickly, and your review keeps quality in your hands.
blocks.hint: Iterating beats both blind trust and starting over.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks {{tool}} for one activity in three levels for a topic you really teach.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that creates one classroom activity in support, core and extension versions. Include the learning goal, grade level, time available and what the support version should offer.
practice.default_context: A Grade 6 teacher needs a 30-minute activity on main idea in a short article for a mixed-level class of 24.

rubric.description: States grade, subject, time and any relevant group needs without naming students.
Names one clear learning goal that all versions aim at.
Asks for support, core and extension and says what the support level should include.

practice.example_good_prompt: Grade 6 English, 30 minutes, 24 students. Goal: students identify the main idea of a short article and support it with two details. Create one activity in three versions: support with sentence starters and a graphic organizer, core, and extension with an unfamiliar text. Keep the goal identical. Add a 2-minute check at the end.

common_mistakes: Learners write one-line prompts without grade, time or goal. Ask what the AI would have to guess.
Learners paste student names or details. Remind them to describe needs generally.
key_points: Context in, usable draft out.
Same goal, different support.
You review and adapt every plan.
follow_up_tasks: Rewrite the prompt "Make a history lesson" with goal, grade, time and one group need.

lessons.goal: Generate quiz questions and a rubric aligned to one objective, and check every answer yourself.
lessons.title: Quizzes, rubrics and exit tickets

blocks.title: Start from the objective
blocks.body:
Quality questions test one objective. Give the AI the objective, grade, question types and number, plus what students have covered. Ask for a mix, such as recall, application and one short explanation.

Example: "Objective: calculate the area of rectangles. Grade 4. Five questions, last one a word problem."

blocks.title: Rubrics and exit tickets
blocks.body: Ask for a rubric with three or four criteria and clear level descriptions in student-friendly words. For an exit ticket, ask for two or three quick questions that show whether students reached the objective today.

blocks.title: Check every key
blocks.body: AI makes factual and math mistakes and states them confidently. It can give a wrong answer key, two correct options or an ambiguous question. Solve each question yourself before students see it. Also check the wording against what you actually taught.

blocks.question: Which request gives you a quiz aligned to your lesson?
options: Write a quiz about fractions.
Objective: compare fractions with unlike denominators. Grade 5. Six multiple-choice questions, plus one question asking students to explain their reasoning.
Write a hard fractions test with an answer key.
blocks.explanation: A clear objective, grade and question mix keep the quiz focused on what you taught.
blocks.hint: Look for the objective and the question types.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What should you check in an AI-generated answer key?
options: That every calculation is correct
That only one option is truly correct in each multiple-choice question
That the quiz looks long enough
That the content matches what you actually taught
blocks.explanation: Wrong math, double-correct options and off-topic content are the common errors. Length is your choice.
blocks.hint: Think about what could be wrong, not how the quiz looks.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this rubric prompt work best.
blocks.prompt: Create a rubric for a Grade 7 paragraph on a historical event. ___
options: Make it fair.
Use four criteria, claim, evidence, organization and grammar, with three levels each, in words a 12-year-old understands.
Add as many criteria as possible.
blocks.explanation: Named criteria, levels and reading level make the rubric usable for both you and students.
blocks.hint: A good rubric names criteria and describes levels.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If AI gives an answer key, you can trust the math.
cards.explanation: AI makes arithmetic and factual errors, so solve each item yourself.

cards.statement: An exit ticket should show whether students reached today's objective.
cards.explanation: Two or three targeted questions give you quick evidence.

cards.statement: You should paste real student quiz results into a public AI tool to find patterns.
cards.explanation: Results can identify students. Use anonymized or summarized data only.

blocks.hint: Ask what can go wrong if you skip checking.

blocks.question: You solve question 4 and get 36, but the AI key says 32. What do you do?
options: Keep the key, the AI is probably right.
Recheck your work, then correct the key if you are right, and review the other items too.
Remove the key and give students no answers.
blocks.explanation: One mistake suggests there may be others, so confirm yourself and review the rest.
blocks.hint: One error is a signal about the rest.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks {{tool}} for an exit ticket and a short rubric for one lesson objective.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that creates a 3-question exit ticket and a 3-criterion rubric for one learning objective. Say how you will check the answer key.
practice.default_context: A Grade 8 science teacher needs an exit ticket and a short rubric on explaining cause and effect in a lab report.

rubric.description: Names one clear learning objective and the grade level.
Asks for a number of questions, a rubric with criteria and levels, and a reading level.
Mentions solving or checking the answer key yourself.

practice.example_good_prompt: Grade 8 science. Objective: students explain cause and effect in a lab result. Create a 3-question exit ticket, one recall, one application and one short explanation, and a rubric with three criteria and three levels in student-friendly words. Give an answer key; I will verify it myself before use.

common_mistakes: Learners skip the objective and ask for a quiz on a topic. Ask which skill the quiz should measure.
Learners trust the answer key. Have them solve two items and compare.
key_points: One objective per quiz.
Rubrics need criteria and level descriptions.
You verify every answer key.
follow_up_tasks: Ask for five math questions, solve them yourself and note any errors in the key.

lessons.goal: Draft rubric-based feedback from anonymized work and talk with students about AI use fairly.
lessons.title: Feedback on student work, and integrity

blocks.title: Remove names first
blocks.body: Student work is personal data. Before using a public AI tool, remove names, IDs, photos and details that identify a child. Replace them with "Student A". Follow your school's policy on which tools you may use at all.

blocks.title: Comments against your rubric
blocks.body: Paste your rubric and the anonymized work. Ask for two strengths, one next step and a comment in plain, kind language, tied to the criteria. You read each comment, edit it and decide the grade yourself.

blocks.title: Talk about AI use
blocks.body: AI detectors are unreliable and can falsely accuse honest students. Instead, set clear rules for when AI is allowed, ask students to note how they used it, and ask them to explain their work in conversation.

blocks.question: What should you do before pasting an essay into a public AI tool?
options: Keep the name so the feedback feels personal.
Remove the name and identifying details, and use a tool your school allows.
Nothing, an essay is just schoolwork, not personal data.
blocks.explanation: Student work can identify a child. Anonymize it and follow school policy.
blocks.hint: Ask what could identify a child if the text is stored.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What belongs in a good feedback prompt?
options: Your rubric criteria
The student's full name and class
A request for strengths and one next step
A request to give the final grade
blocks.explanation: Rubric and structure give useful comments. Names add risk, and the grade is your decision.
blocks.hint: Two options hand over data or decisions that belong to you.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that best completes your class AI policy.
blocks.prompt: You may use AI to brainstorm ideas. ___
options: Anything else counts as cheating, with no exceptions.
Add a short note saying how you used it, and be ready to explain your work to me.
I will run every essay through a detector.
blocks.explanation: Clear rules, disclosure and conversation are fairer than relying on detectors.
blocks.hint: The best policy is specific and keeps a human conversation.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: An AI detector score is enough proof that a student cheated.
cards.explanation: Detectors make errors, especially with some writing styles. Talk to the student.

cards.statement: AI can draft comments, but the teacher decides the grade.
cards.explanation: Grading judgment and responsibility stay with you.

cards.statement: Asking students to explain their work orally helps show their own understanding.
cards.explanation: A conversation reveals understanding better than a score.

blocks.hint: Who is accountable for a grade?

blocks.question: AI suggests the comment "Great job!" for a weak essay. What do you do?
options: Send it, it saves time.
Rewrite it to match the rubric: name a real strength and one clear next step.
Ask the AI to write a longer comment with more praise.
blocks.explanation: Feedback must reflect the actual work. You edit AI drafts to be accurate and specific.
blocks.hint: Compare the comment with what the student actually wrote.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks {{tool}} for rubric-based feedback on an anonymized student paragraph.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a prompt for {{tool}} to draft feedback on one anonymized piece of student work. Include your rubric, the structure of the comment and who makes the final grade.
practice.default_context: A Grade 9 English teacher has 30 paragraph responses to comment on and a three-criterion rubric.

rubric.description: Uses anonymized work, such as Student A, and no personal details.
Ties comments to named criteria.
States the teacher edits comments and decides the grade.

practice.example_good_prompt: Below is an anonymized paragraph by Student A and my rubric (claim, evidence, clarity). Draft feedback in kind, plain language, two strengths, one next step, tied to the criteria. Do not give a grade; I will review and decide.

common_mistakes: Learners leave names or school details in pasted work. Have them anonymize first.
Learners ask AI for a grade. Redirect to comments only.
key_points: Anonymize before you paste.
AI drafts comments, you decide the grade.
Use clear rules and conversation, not detectors.
follow_up_tasks: Write three sentences for a class AI policy.

courses.title: AI in Your Office Tools
courses.description: Use the AI inside your email, documents, spreadsheets and slides to finish routine work faster, while checking the output and protecting company data.

lessons.goal: Draft, reshape and summarize emails and documents with built-in AI, using only approved tools.
lessons.title: Email and documents with built-in AI

blocks.title: Draft from facts, not from nothing
blocks.body: If your company has turned them on, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Gemini in Google Workspace can draft inside your email and documents. Give them the facts: who reads it, what happened, what you need and by when. A reply to a late supplier needs the order number, missed date and new deadline.

blocks.title: Reshape and condense
blocks.body: Ask the AI to make a draft warmer, shorter or more formal, or to summarize a long thread into decisions, open questions and owners. Read the original for anything about money, deadlines or commitments.

blocks.title: Approved tools versus personal accounts
blocks.body: Company-approved tools usually run under your organization's data rules. A personal ChatGPT account does not. Never paste client details, contracts or staff data into a personal account. Unsure? Ask IT first.

blocks.question: Your supplier delivered late. Which request gives the built-in AI the best starting point for a reply?
options: Write a reply to this supplier.
Write a firm, polite reply: order 4471 arrived 5 days late; I need delivery by Friday and a call this week.
Make my email better.
blocks.explanation: The AI cannot know your facts. The problem, deadline and ask let it draft something close to ready.
blocks.hint: Look for the option with facts the AI could not guess.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. AI summarized a 40-message thread. What do you check before acting?
options: Dates and deadlines
Amounts and numbers
Whether the summary sounds confident
Who agreed to do what
blocks.explanation: Summaries slip on dates, numbers and ownership. A confident tone proves nothing.
blocks.hint: Think about the details that cause real problems if wrong.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that best completes the follow-up request.
blocks.prompt: Rewrite your draft for a senior client. ___ Keep every fact the same.
options: Make it good.
Use a formal tone, under 120 words, no casual phrases.
Change everything.
blocks.explanation: A good follow-up names the tone and length, and says what must stay unchanged.
blocks.hint: Pick the instruction you could measure when you read the result.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A company-approved AI tool and a personal ChatGPT account follow the same data rules.
cards.explanation: Approved tools are set up under your organization's agreements. Personal accounts are not.

cards.statement: If a document contains client details, ask which AI tool is approved before using it.
cards.explanation: Asking is cheap. A data leak is not.

cards.statement: Replacing a client's name with "Client A" makes any contract safe to paste into any tool.
cards.explanation: Other details can still identify the client or be confidential. Use an approved tool or ask first.

blocks.hint: Ask who controls the data after you paste it.

blocks.question: Your company has no approved AI tool yet. You need to summarize a client complaint email. What is the best move?
options: Paste it into your personal AI account, since it is only a summary.
Remove the client's name only, then paste it.
Ask your manager or IT what is allowed, and summarize it yourself.
blocks.explanation: Names are only part of the risk. Complaint details can identify a client too, so check the rules first.
blocks.hint: When the rules are unclear, who should decide?

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give your built-in AI to draft a message for a real situation at work. Use made-up details instead of real names.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}} and use {{tool}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write the request you would give the AI to draft a message about this. Include the reader, the key facts, the tone and the length. Add one line on what you would check before sending.
practice.default_context: You are an office coordinator who must reply to a colleague who missed a deadline for a shared report.

rubric.description: Names the situation, the reader and the specific details the draft needs.
Asks for a tone and a length or structure.
Says what will be verified before sending and avoids real confidential data.

practice.example_good_prompt: Draft a polite but firm email to a colleague who missed Tuesday's deadline for the shared sales report. Say I need it by noon Thursday, keep it under 100 words, no blame. Before sending I will check the dates and the tone.

common_mistakes: Learners write vague requests like "write an email". Ask for the reader, facts and deadline.
Learners send AI summaries unchecked. Have them find one detail in the original thread.
Learners think a personal account is fine for a quick task. Ask who controls pasted data afterwards.
key_points: Give facts, reader, tone and length.
Check dates, numbers and commitments yourself.
Use company-approved tools for work data.
follow_up_tasks: Take a short email you wrote and ask AI for a formal and a friendly version. Note what changed in the facts.

lessons.goal: Get formulas explained or written, clean messy data and analyze an export, then spot-check the results.
lessons.title: Spreadsheets with AI

blocks.title: Explain and write formulas
blocks.body: Paste a formula you inherited and ask the AI to explain it step by step. Or describe what you want: "Sum column C where column A says North and column B is March." Say what each column holds, and test the formula on rows you can calculate by hand.

blocks.title: Clean messy data
blocks.body: Exports often have mixed date formats, extra spaces and names written three ways. Ask the AI how to fix one problem at a time, in a copy of your sheet. Never clean your only version.

blocks.title: Analyze, then spot-check
blocks.body: Ask for trends, outliers or a summary of an export. The AI can miscount or skip rows without warning. Check the row count, recalculate one total and look at the biggest and smallest values. Do not share names, salaries or other personal data with a tool that is not approved.

blocks.question: Which request is most likely to produce a working formula?
options: Make a formula for my sales.
In column D, sum the amounts in column C only where column A is North and column B is March.
Calculate everything in my sheet.
blocks.explanation: Naming the columns and conditions removes guesswork.
blocks.hint: The AI cannot see your intent, only your words.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. The AI gives a total for 500 rows. Which checks make sense?
options: Compare the row count in the answer with the sheet
Recalculate the total with a simple sum yourself
Trust it, because it is a calculation
Check the largest and smallest values for oddities
blocks.explanation: Quick manual checks catch skipped rows and misread numbers.
blocks.hint: Which checks take two minutes and use only the sheet?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this cleaning request work.
blocks.prompt: Column B holds dates typed in different formats. ___ Do not change any other column.
options: Fix it.
Give me a formula that converts them all to day/month/year, and list any cells it cannot convert.
Make the dates pretty.
blocks.explanation: One clear format and a list of failures make problems visible.
blocks.hint: Good requests also expose what could not be fixed.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: An HR export with names and salaries should not go into an unapproved AI tool.
cards.explanation: Personal data should stay in approved systems. Use an approved tool, or remove identifying data and ask first.

cards.statement: It is wise to clean your only copy of a dataset directly.
cards.explanation: Work on a copy so you can compare and undo.

cards.statement: AI can explain a formula you did not write.
cards.explanation: This is a safe, useful task. Still test the formula on a few rows.

blocks.hint: Think about what you could not get back.

blocks.question: AI says your top-selling region is West, but you remember East being higher. What do you do?
options: Accept it, since the AI looked at all the data.
Filter the sheet by region, sum each one yourself and compare.
Ask the AI again until it says East.
blocks.explanation: Your own check settles it. Re-asking until you hear what you expect proves nothing.
blocks.hint: Which option uses evidence from the sheet?

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give an AI assistant about a spreadsheet from your work, and describe how you would check the answer.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}} and use {{tool}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request asking the AI for a formula, a data cleanup or a quick analysis related to a spreadsheet you use. Describe the columns, say what you want back, and explain how you would spot-check the result. Use made-up data only.
practice.default_context: You have a monthly expenses export with columns for date, department, supplier and amount, and you need totals per department.

rubric.description: Names the columns and what they contain.
Says exactly what result or format is wanted.
Names a concrete check, such as recalculating one total or comparing row counts.

practice.example_good_prompt: My sheet has columns A date, B department, C supplier, D amount. Write a formula that totals D for each department, and list any rows where the amount is empty. I will check by filtering one department and adding it up myself.

common_mistakes: Learners do not describe columns. Ask what each one holds.
Learners accept totals unchecked. Have them recalculate one number by hand.
Learners upload real personal data. Remind them to use approved tools or leave the data out.
key_points: Describe the columns and the goal.
Work on a copy of your data.
Always spot-check totals and counts.
follow_up_tasks: Ask AI to explain a formula from your own sheet, then rebuild its result on two rows by hand.

lessons.goal: Turn rough notes into a presentation or report by building an outline first, then content, then a version tuned for the audience.
lessons.title: From notes to a presentation or report

blocks.title: Outline first
blocks.body: Do not ask for a full deck from a pile of notes. Paste the notes and ask for an outline: the audience, the one message they should leave with, and four to six sections. Change the outline until the structure is right.

blocks.title: Then slides or sections
blocks.body: Once the outline is right, ask for one part at a time. For slides, ask for a title that states the point and three short bullets. For a report, ask for a paragraph per section. Tell the AI to use only your notes and to mark any gap instead of inventing a number.

blocks.title: Tighten for the audience
blocks.body: Your manager wants decisions and costs. A client wants benefits. A team wants next steps. Ask for the content rewritten for one reader and a time limit, then check every number, name and claim against your notes.

blocks.question: You have messy meeting notes and need a deck for your director. What is the best first request?
options: Make a 20-slide deck from these notes.
Suggest an outline for a 10-minute update to my director: one key message, five sections.
Make my notes look professional.
blocks.explanation: An outline lets you fix the structure while changes are still cheap.
blocks.hint: What is easiest to correct before any slides exist?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. AI turned your notes into slides. What do you check?
options: Every number against your notes
Whether any claim appears that is not in your notes
Whether the slides look modern
Names and dates
blocks.explanation: Slides can add invented facts or change figures. Looks can wait until the facts are right.
blocks.hint: Compare the output with your source, not with your taste.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that best tunes this section for its reader.
blocks.prompt: Rewrite this section for the finance director. ___ Use only the figures in my notes.
options: Make it better.
Lead with total cost and the decision needed, and cut it to three bullets.
Add more detail.
blocks.explanation: The reader's priority and a size limit shape the rewrite. Restricting it to your figures prevents invention.
blocks.hint: A finance director cares about cost and decisions.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Asking the AI to mark gaps is safer than letting it fill missing numbers.
cards.explanation: A marked gap is visible. An invented number looks like a fact.

cards.statement: A slide title should state the point, not just the topic.
cards.explanation: A title like "Revenue grew 8% in Q2" tells the audience more than "Revenue".

cards.statement: Slides built from your notes need no checking if they look polished.
cards.explanation: Polish hides errors. Compare every figure and claim with your notes.

blocks.hint: Ask what a reader sees on the slide.

blocks.question: The first outline buries the decision you need from your manager at the end. What next?
options: Start over with a new chat.
Ask the AI to move the decision to the first section and shorten the background.
Keep it, since the AI chose that order for a reason.
blocks.explanation: Refining the outline beats starting over. You know what the audience needs.
blocks.hint: You are the expert on the audience.

practice.instructions: Write your outline request for a short presentation or report. Name the audience, the key message and what the AI should do about missing facts.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}} and use {{tool}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request that turns rough notes into an outline for a presentation or report on this topic. Include the audience, the key message, the number of sections and a limit on length. Add an instruction on what the AI should do about missing facts.
practice.default_context: You must present a quarterly update from rough notes to your manager, who has 10 minutes and wants decisions and costs.

rubric.description: Says who the reader is and what they should take away.
Requests an outline with sections and a length or time limit.
Tells the AI to use only the supplied notes and mark gaps.

practice.example_good_prompt: Here are my notes (pasted below). Create an outline for a 10-minute update to my manager. The key message is that we need budget approval. Give five sections, put the decision first, use only my notes, and mark any missing figure as [gap].

common_mistakes: Learners request a whole deck at once. Steer them to outline first.
Learners let the AI add numbers. Teach "use only my notes, mark gaps".
Learners skip the audience. Ask who reads it and what they decide.
key_points: Outline first, then content, then tighten.
Say who the audience is and the one key message.
Check every number against your notes.
follow_up_tasks: Take one slide and ask for versions for a manager and a client. Note what each version put first.

courses.title: Automate Your Routine
courses.description: Turn your best prompts into reusable templates, build a custom assistant for one recurring task and connect AI to a simple no-code flow with a human check.

lessons.goal: Turn a prompt that worked into a reusable template and keep it in an organized library.
lessons.title: Turn good prompts into a template library

blocks.title: From one prompt to a template
blocks.body:
When a prompt works, do not leave it in your chat history. Replace the parts that change each time with placeholders in square brackets, such as [Client] or [Deadline]. Keep the parts that made it work: tone, structure and length.

Example: "Write an email to [Client] asking for [Document] by [Date]. Friendly, under 90 words, end with one next step."

blocks.title: Build a small library
blocks.body: Keep templates in one place you open daily, such as a notes app or a shared document. Group them by task: Email, Reports, Meetings. Give each a clear name and a one-line note on when to use it. If you cannot find a template in ten seconds, you will stop using it.

blocks.title: Improve it with use
blocks.body: After each use, notice what you fixed by hand. If you shorten the answer every time, add the length to the template. If a rule was ignored, state it more plainly. Date each change and keep the best version.

blocks.question: Which part of a working prompt should become a placeholder?
options: The tone and length that made the result good.
The client name and deadline, which change every time.
Every word, so the template fits any task.
The instruction to keep the answer short.
blocks.explanation: Placeholders hold what changes. The instructions that made the prompt work stay fixed.
blocks.hint: Ask what is different each time you use the prompt.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What helps a template library stay useful?
options: Grouping templates by task.
A one-line note on when to use each one.
The date you last improved it.
Real client details left in from the last use.
blocks.explanation: Grouping, notes and dates make templates easy to find and trust. Real client details do not belong in a saved template.
blocks.hint: Think about finding and trusting a template months later.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this template reusable.
blocks.prompt: Summarize [Meeting notes] for [Manager]. ___
options: Make it good.
Give 3 bullets, then one line on open decisions.
Use last week's notes as a guide.
blocks.explanation: A fixed format gives consistent results every time. The other options are vague or tied to one week.
blocks.hint: Choose what you want every single time you run it.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A template swaps only what changes and keeps the instructions that worked.
cards.explanation: That is what makes the result consistent.

cards.statement: Once a template works, you should never change it.
cards.explanation: Needs shift, so review templates and improve them.

cards.statement: If you fix the same thing by hand every time, add it to the template.
cards.explanation: Repeated fixes show an instruction is missing.

blocks.hint: Ask what a repeated fix tells you.

blocks.question: Your weekly report template always gives long summaries, and you trim them each week. What is the best step?
options: Keep trimming by hand.
Add a limit such as 5 bullets to the template.
Delete the template and write a new prompt each week.
Ask for a longer summary and cut it later.
blocks.explanation: Moving your repeated fix into the template saves the work every week.
blocks.hint: Where could the fix live so you do it only once?

practice.instructions: Turn one prompt for a real recurring task into a template with placeholders and give it a library entry.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a reusable prompt template for {{tool}} for this task. Use at least three placeholders in square brackets, fixed instructions for format and tone, and no private data. Add a library entry: a name, when to use it, and one improvement you would make after the first use.
practice.default_context: You are an office coordinator who sends a weekly status email to clients about their open requests.

rubric.description: Changing details are placeholders and the instructions that make it work stay fixed.
The template states format, length or tone so results are consistent.
Gives a clear name, a use note and a realistic improvement idea, without private data.

practice.example_good_prompt: Template: Write a status email to [Client] about [Request]. Current status: [Status]. Next step and date: [Next step]. Friendly, under 100 words, one clear next step. Library entry: Weekly client status, use every Friday, after first use I would add a subject line rule.

common_mistakes: Making everything a placeholder. Ask which instructions made the prompt work and keep those fixed.
Leaving real names in the saved template. Show how to replace them with placeholders.
key_points: A template keeps what worked and swaps only what changes.
Organize by task and add a use note so you can find it fast.
Improve a template after each use.
follow_up_tasks: Take your last good prompt, mark what changes each time, and rewrite it with placeholders.

lessons.goal: Set up a custom assistant with instructions and reference documents, and test it on real past cases.
lessons.title: Build a custom assistant for one recurring task

blocks.title: One assistant, one task
blocks.body: A custom assistant is a saved setup: your instructions plus your reference documents. Tools use different names, but the idea is the same. It works best for one narrow, repeated task, such as answering parent questions about homework policy. "Help with everything" gives uneven results.

blocks.title: What goes in
blocks.body: Instructions say who it helps, what it does, the format, and what it must not do. Add a rule for gaps: "If the documents do not cover it, say so." Documents are your policy, FAQ or sample good answers. Upload only what your company allows, and keep them current.

blocks.title: Test before you trust it
blocks.body: Collect 5 to 10 real past cases, including one tricky one. Run each and compare with what you actually sent. Where it is wrong, fix the instructions or documents and run again. Only then use it on live work, and still read every answer.

blocks.question: Which task suits a custom assistant best?
options: Answering the same questions about your return policy every week.
Helping with anything your team might ask.
Writing a one-time farewell speech.
Deciding which candidate to hire.
blocks.explanation: A narrow, repeated task with a clear source document gives consistent results.
blocks.hint: Look for a task that repeats and has a written source.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What belongs in a custom assistant's setup?
options: A rule to say when the answer is not in the documents.
Your current policy document.
The format you want for answers.
Old policy versions beside the current one.
blocks.explanation: Clear rules, current sources and a format shape good answers. Old versions can conflict.
blocks.hint: Choose what guides answers without adding risk.

blocks.question: Pick the instruction that makes this assistant safest.
blocks.prompt: You answer candidate questions for our HR team. Use only the attached process guide. ___
options: If the guide does not cover the question, say so and suggest contacting HR.
If unsure, give your best guess so the candidate is not left waiting.
Add helpful details from general knowledge.
blocks.explanation: A gap rule stops the assistant from inventing answers about your process.
blocks.hint: What should happen when the guide has no answer?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Testing on real past cases shows weak spots before anyone outside sees them.
cards.explanation: You can compare its answers with what you actually sent.

cards.statement: If the first three tests look fine, you can stop testing.
cards.explanation: Include a tricky case, because that is where assistants usually fail.

cards.statement: An outdated document can make the assistant give outdated answers.
cards.explanation: It relies on what you give it, so update documents when policies change.

blocks.hint: Think about where mistakes would first appear.

blocks.question: In testing, your assistant invents a refund rule that is not in your policy. What is the best fix?
options: Ignore it, because it was only one error.
Add an instruction to use only the policy, then run the test again.
Switch tools and hope for better.
Stop testing and use it carefully.
blocks.explanation: Fix the instructions, then re-run the same case to confirm the problem is gone.
blocks.hint: What would stop it from going beyond the policy?

practice.instructions: Design a custom assistant for one recurring task and plan how to test it on real past cases.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Design a custom assistant for {{tool}} or a similar tool for one recurring task related to this pain. Write its instructions, list which reference documents you would give it, and describe how you would test it on real past cases. Do not include confidential data.
practice.default_context: You are a school administrator who answers parents' questions about absences and homework policy every week.

rubric.description: Names one task and gives clear instructions on audience, format and limits.
Lists suitable reference documents and tells the assistant what to do when the answer is missing.
Plans to test on several real past cases, including a tricky one, and to check answers before use.

practice.example_good_prompt: Task: answer parents' questions about absences. Instructions: You help parents of our school. Use only the attached attendance policy and FAQ. Answer in under 80 words, politely. If the documents do not cover it, say so and suggest contacting the office. Never discuss other students. Test: run 8 past parent emails, including one unusual case, compare with my sent replies, fix the instructions, then re-run.

common_mistakes: Building one assistant for many tasks. Help the learner pick one narrow task.
Skipping the gap rule. Ask what the assistant should do when the documents are silent.
key_points: Instructions plus reference documents define the assistant.
Test on real past cases, including a tricky one.
Keep documents current and still read every answer.
follow_up_tasks: Pick three past cases and write what a correct answer would look like for each.

lessons.goal: Design a small flow with a trigger, an AI step and an action, with a human check before anything reaches people.
lessons.title: Chain AI into a simple no-code flow

blocks.title: Trigger, AI step, action
blocks.body:
No-code tools like Zapier, Make or Power Automate connect apps without programming. A flow has three parts. The **trigger** starts it. The **AI step** processes text. The **action** does something with the result.

Example: a new form response arrives (trigger), AI summarizes it (AI step), the summary is saved to a notes page (action).

blocks.title: Keep a human check
blocks.body: Before anything reaches customers, students or candidates, the flow should stop for you. Send the AI output to a draft folder or an approval step, then review and send it yourself. A wrong message that goes out automatically cannot be taken back.

blocks.title: Start small and low-risk
blocks.body: Pick one flow where a mistake costs little, such as summaries sent only to you. Test it with sample data, then watch it for a week before adding steps. Check which data the tool shares with which app, and use only tools your company approves.

blocks.question: In this flow, what is the trigger? "A form is submitted, AI drafts a reply, the draft is saved to your Drafts folder."
options: AI drafts a reply.
A form is submitted.
The draft is saved.
You read the draft.
blocks.explanation: The trigger is the event that starts the flow. The drafting is the AI step and saving is the action.
blocks.hint: Which event happens first and starts everything else?

blocks.question: Which is the best first flow to build?
options: Email a personalized offer to every new lead automatically.
Summarize new form responses into a private page only you see.
Reply to all parent emails automatically.
Send weekly figures to clients with no review.
blocks.explanation: The output stays with you, so a mistake costs little while you learn.
blocks.hint: Look for the flow where an error reaches nobody.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which habits make a flow safer?
options: Sending AI output to a draft or approval step first.
Testing with sample data before using real data.
Checking which data is shared with which app.
Turning on auto-send once it has worked twice.
blocks.explanation: Review, testing and data awareness reduce risk. Two good runs do not prove a flow is reliable.
blocks.hint: Choose habits that catch problems before people see them.

blocks.question: Pick the action that keeps a human in control.
blocks.prompt: New feedback form arrives, AI writes a 3-bullet summary, then ___
options: the summary is emailed to every customer.
the summary is saved as a draft for you to review.
the original form is deleted.
blocks.explanation: A draft waits for your review, so nothing reaches people without your check.
blocks.hint: Which step lets you look before anything goes out?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Every step in a flow needs to use AI.
cards.explanation: AI is one step. Triggers and actions are ordinary automation.

cards.statement: A flow that emails customers should have a person approve each message.
cards.explanation: AI can be wrong, and sent messages cannot be undone.

cards.statement: Start with your most important process to learn quickly.
cards.explanation: Start with a low-risk flow so mistakes stay small.

blocks.hint: Think about the cost of a mistake at each step.

practice.instructions: Design one small, low-risk flow for a routine task, with a human check before anything reaches people.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Design a small no-code flow that could use {{tool}} or a similar AI tool for one step. Describe the trigger, the AI step with its instruction, and the action. Say where you review the result before it reaches anyone, and how you would test it first.
practice.default_context: You are a small-business owner who receives customer inquiries through a web form and wants help with first replies.

rubric.description: Names a clear trigger, an AI step with an instruction and an action.
Places a review or approval step before anything is sent to other people.
Starts with a low-risk scope, plans a test with sample data and avoids confidential data.

practice.example_good_prompt: Trigger: a new inquiry arrives in the web form. AI step: summarize it in 3 bullets and draft a polite reply using only our FAQ. Action: save both as a draft in my inbox, never send. I review and send the reply myself. First I test with five made-up inquiries for a week.

common_mistakes: Letting the flow send messages directly. Ask who reads the output before it goes out.
Starting with a big process. Help the learner shrink it to one low-risk flow.
key_points: A flow is a trigger, an AI step and an action.
Keep a human check before anything reaches people.
Start small and test with sample data.
follow_up_tasks: Write one routine task as trigger, AI step and action in three short lines.

courses.title: ChatGPT for Work
courses.description: Use ChatGPT with your own files, keep your context saved and build a reusable assistant for a task you repeat every week.

lessons.goal: Ask ChatGPT questions about a document or spreadsheet, get quotes as evidence and check them before you reuse the answer.
lessons.title: Ask questions about your own files

blocks.title: Give it the source
blocks.body: ChatGPT can read a document or spreadsheet you add to the conversation, so it works from your file, not from memory. Typical uses: summarize a policy, compare two contracts, find the slowest month in a sales sheet. File support depends on your account and company setup.

blocks.title: Ask for quotes
blocks.body: A summary can hide mistakes. Ask: "Answer only from this file. Quote the sentence you rely on. If the file does not say, tell me." Now each claim has evidence you can find, and gaps are named instead of guessed.

blocks.title: Check, then reuse
blocks.body: Open the quoted passage and read it in context. For spreadsheets, spot-check a total by hand. Also check what you upload: contracts, student records and candidate files may be off limits. Data handling differs by account and company, so follow your rules.

blocks.question: You uploaded a supplier contract. Which question gives you an answer you can verify fastest?
options: What are the main risks here?
What is the notice period for ending it? Quote the clause you used.
Is this contract fair to us?
Summarize everything important.
blocks.explanation: A specific question plus a quote lets you confirm the clause in seconds. The others ask for judgment with nothing to check.
blocks.hint: Which question leaves you something to look up in the file?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that keeps the answer tied to your file.
blocks.prompt: Which employees on the attached rota work over 40 hours in week 3? ___
options: Add what you know about labor rules too.
Use only the file, quote the rows, and say so if data is missing.
Give your best guess if you are unsure.
blocks.explanation: Limiting the source and asking for the rows makes errors easy to spot.
blocks.hint: Which option limits where the answer may come from?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: An answer based on your uploaded file is certainly correct.
cards.explanation: It can still misread a table or skip a clause.

cards.statement: Asking for a quote makes a wrong answer easier to catch.
cards.explanation: You can compare the quote with the original document.

cards.statement: You can skip checking totals because the file is your own data.
cards.explanation: Calculations can go wrong. Recompute a few by hand.

blocks.hint: Think about who is responsible for the result.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which steps make an upload safer?
options: Check that your company allows this kind of file in this tool.
Remove personal details the task does not need.
Upload it first and check the rules later.
Use your company-approved account, not a personal one.
blocks.explanation: Permission, minimal data and the approved account come before the upload.
blocks.hint: Which steps happen before the file leaves your computer?

blocks.question: ChatGPT quotes a refund deadline from an uploaded policy. What do you do before telling a customer?
options: Send it, since it has a quote.
Ask ChatGPT to confirm it again.
Find the quoted sentence and read it in context.
Remove the quote and keep the deadline.
blocks.explanation: A quote points to the evidence. Reading the original confirms it.
blocks.hint: Imagine the customer disputes the deadline and you are asked to show where it comes from.

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that asks about a file you could upload, requires quotes and tells the assistant what to do when the file lacks the answer.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Describe a document or spreadsheet related to this pain that your company would allow you to upload to {{tool}}. Write a prompt that asks one specific question about it, requires quoted evidence and says what to do if the answer is missing. Add one line on how you would check the result.
practice.default_context: You are an office manager who needs the cancellation terms from a supplier contract.

rubric.description: The prompt says which file to use and limits the answer to it.
The prompt asks for quotes or the rows used, and a clear answer when the file does not say.
The learner says how they would verify the answer and keeps private data out.

practice.example_good_prompt: Using only the attached supplier contract, tell me the notice period for cancelling and any early-exit fee. Quote the clause for each. If the contract does not say, answer "not stated". I will read each quoted clause in the original before I reply to the supplier.

common_mistakes: Asking for a general summary and trusting it. Steer toward a specific question with a quote.
Uploading files without checking company rules. Ask what their policy says and what could be removed.
key_points: Ground the answer in the file and ask for the passage used.
Read the quote in the original before reuse.
Upload only what your company allows.
follow_up_tasks: Take one page from a real document and write three questions that each require a quote.

lessons.goal: Save your role, audience and style so you stop repeating them, and organize recurring work into separate spaces.
lessons.title: Set your context once

blocks.title: Stop repeating yourself
blocks.body: A new conversation often starts without your background, so you retype "I am an HR manager, write for employees, keep it short" again and again. ChatGPT can store standing instructions about you and how you want answers. Write them once: role, usual reader, tone, formats you like. Availability varies by account and company setup.

blocks.title: Keep a space per area
blocks.body: Mixed topics confuse answers. ChatGPT may offer projects, which group related chats, files and instructions in one place. Keep one per recurring area, such as "Monthly reports" or "Recruiting". Everything in it shares the same background, so you add only what is new. Availability varies.

blocks.title: Keep it short and safe
blocks.body: Instructions apply to every chat, so use only what is always true. Avoid client names, salaries or other confidential details. Put area-specific rules in that area's project. Review the text now and then, because your work changes.

blocks.question: Which line belongs in your standing instructions?
options: Write emails to our customer Mrs Keller about her invoice.
I am a marketing lead. Write in plain, friendly English, under 120 words.
The Q3 budget is 48,000.
Remember this week's meeting agenda.
blocks.explanation: Role, style and length are always true. The others are one-off or contain details that do not belong everywhere.
blocks.hint: Choose what is true for almost every task you do.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which are good reasons to create a separate project?
options: You write a weekly newsletter with the same style each time.
You handle parent emails and want shared tone rules.
You want to ask one unrelated question.
You review contracts and want related files together.
blocks.explanation: Projects fit recurring work with shared files or tone. A one-off question needs none.
blocks.hint: Think about work you come back to again and again.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes these standing instructions useful.
blocks.prompt: I teach Year 8 science. ___ Never include student names.
options: Make my lessons great.
Write for 13-year-olds in short sentences and ask before adding a topic.
Always give long, detailed answers.
blocks.explanation: It states reader, style and a working rule. Vague wishes change little.
blocks.hint: Which option changes what the answer looks like?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Saved instructions mean you can skip checking answers.
cards.explanation: Context improves style and fit. It does not make facts correct.

cards.statement: Rules for one client belong in that client's project, not in general instructions.
cards.explanation: General instructions apply everywhere, so keep them to what is always true.

cards.statement: Standing instructions are a good place for client data.
cards.explanation: Keep sensitive information out. Instructions shape every chat.

cards.statement: Review your instructions when your role changes.
cards.explanation: Outdated instructions quietly shape answers.

blocks.hint: Ask whether it is always true and safe to store.

blocks.question: Recruiting answers keep sounding like your marketing work. What fixes this best?
options: Add recruiting rules to your general instructions.
Explain the difference at the start of every chat.
Keep recruiting in its own project with its own instructions and files.
Tell it to ignore marketing in each chat.
blocks.explanation: A dedicated space keeps background separate without bloating the general text.
blocks.hint: Which option separates the two areas?

practice.instructions: Write standing instructions about yourself, then name one project you would create and what it would hold.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write short standing instructions for {{tool}}: your role, your usual reader, tone, preferred format and one rule. Then name one project for work related to this pain and say what instructions or files it would hold. Include no confidential data.
practice.default_context: You are an office coordinator who writes weekly updates to staff and monthly updates to clients.

rubric.description: The instructions state role, reader, tone and format without one-off details.
The project covers one recurring area and says what it holds.
No confidential or personal data appears in the instructions.

practice.example_good_prompt: Instructions: I am an office coordinator. My readers are busy staff and clients. Write in plain English, friendly and brief, with a short bulleted summary first. Ask me before adding facts. Project: Client monthly updates, holding the update template, the tone rules for clients and last month's approved update.

common_mistakes: Stuffing instructions with case details. Ask whether each line is true every time.
Putting confidential data in instructions. Suggest placeholders instead.
key_points: Write role, reader and style once.
One project per recurring area of work.
Context improves fit, not accuracy.
follow_up_tasks: Sort ten facts about your work into always-true, project-only or never-store.

lessons.goal: Design and test a focused custom assistant for a task you repeat, using clear instructions and example inputs and outputs.
lessons.title: Build a reusable assistant for one task

blocks.title: One task, one assistant
blocks.body: If you paste the same long prompt every week, consider a reusable assistant: instructions defined once, then applied to new inputs. Examples: turn raw meeting notes into a standard summary, or draft replies to common customer questions. Whether you can create or share one depends on your account and company setup.

blocks.title: Instructions and examples
blocks.body: Write what it does, who reads the result, the format and what it must never do. Add one or two example inputs with the output you want. Examples show style better than description. Include a rule for missing information: ask, do not invent.

blocks.title: Test before you trust
blocks.body: Run it on five realistic cases, with personal details removed, including a messy one and one with missing details. Compare each output with what you would write yourself, and fix the instructions where it fails. Keep it to one task.

blocks.question: Which is the best scope for a reusable assistant?
options: Help with anything in the office.
Turn raw weekly sales notes into our 5-line team summary.
Handle HR, finance and marketing questions.
Be smart and professional.
blocks.explanation: One clear task with a known input and output is easy to test. Broad assistants are inconsistent.
blocks.hint: Which one has a clear input and a clear output?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What belongs in the instructions of a customer-reply assistant?
options: The tone and maximum length of a reply.
One example question with the reply you would approve.
What to do when the customer's question is not covered.
Real customer names and account numbers for reference.
blocks.explanation: Tone, an example and a rule for gaps shape every reply. Customer data does not belong there.
blocks.hint: Choose what stays true for every customer.

blocks.question: Pick the rule that makes the assistant safer on incomplete input.
blocks.prompt: You turn meeting notes into a summary with decisions and owners. ___
options: Fill in any missing owners with the most likely person.
If an owner or date is missing, write 'owner not stated' and list the gap at the end.
Never mention what is missing.
blocks.explanation: Flagging gaps lets you fix them. Guessing creates errors that look finished.
blocks.hint: What should happen when a detail is not there?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Testing on one easy example is enough before sharing the assistant.
cards.explanation: Real inputs are messier. Try several.

cards.statement: Example inputs and outputs help the assistant match your style.
cards.explanation: An example shows format and tone better than a description.

cards.statement: Once the assistant works, its output needs no checking.
cards.explanation: It can still miss details. You remain responsible for what you send.

blocks.hint: Think about messy, real cases.

blocks.question: Your assistant writes replies that are too long on two of five tests. What do you do?
options: Accept it, since three tests were fine.
Add a length limit and an example to the instructions, then retest.
Create a new assistant for each test.
Tell colleagues to shorten every reply.
blocks.explanation: Fix the instructions, then rerun the same cases.
blocks.hint: Where does a repeated problem get fixed once?

practice.instructions: Design a focused assistant for one repeated task and plan how you would test it.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Design a reusable assistant in {{tool}} for one repeated task connected to this pain. Write its instructions: task, reader, format, one rule for missing information and one thing it must not do. Add one example input and output, and name two test cases you would run.
practice.default_context: You are a team assistant who turns rough meeting notes into a short summary with decisions and next steps every week.

rubric.description: The assistant has one clear task, reader and output format.
Instructions include a missing-information rule, a limit and an example input and output.
The learner names test cases that include a messy or incomplete input.

practice.example_good_prompt: Task: turn rough meeting notes into a summary for the team. Format: three bullet decisions, then a table of next steps with owner and date. If an owner or date is missing, write 'not stated'. Do not add facts. Example: input 'Anna to send the offer Friday, budget agreed' gives decision 'Budget agreed' and next step 'Send offer, Anna, Friday'. Tests: one messy set of notes, one with no owners.

common_mistakes: Building one assistant for many tasks. Ask them to pick the single most repeated one.
Testing only on a clean example. Ask for a messy, incomplete test case.
key_points: One assistant, one task.
Instructions plus examples plus a rule for gaps.
Test on real cases and keep checking output.
follow_up_tasks: Write instructions for an assistant that drafts a reply to the question you get most often.

courses.title: Gemini in Google Workspace
courses.description: Use Gemini inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides and Drive to draft, summarize, analyze and build first versions faster, then check every result against your sources.

lessons.goal: Draft replies in your own voice, summarize long threads and documents, and rewrite text for a new reader while checking facts and commitments.
lessons.title: Gmail and Docs: write, summarize, rewrite

blocks.title: Availability and your voice
blocks.body: Gemini works inside your mail and documents, but availability depends on your account type and organization settings. If you have it, it drafts from a short instruction. Follow company data rules for what you let it read. To sound like you, give a sample: "Match the tone of my last email to this client: friendly, short, no exclamation marks."

blocks.title: Summarize, then rewrite
blocks.body: Ask for a long thread as decisions, open questions and owners. Ask for a document rewritten for another reader, such as a plain-language parent version. Say what must stay unchanged, like dates and amounts.

blocks.title: Check what you will be held to
blocks.body: A summary can drop a condition or give a promise to the wrong person. Before you act, confirm dates, amounts and commitments in the original. If it says "Maria will send the contract Friday", check that Maria said it.

blocks.question: You want Gemini to reply to a client in your usual style. Which request works best?
options: Reply to this email.
Reply to this email. Match the tone of my earlier message below: warm, three sentences, no jargon. Confirm the meeting is Thursday at 10.
Write a better reply than I would.
blocks.explanation: A tone sample and facts to confirm keep the draft yours and correct.
blocks.hint: What does Gemini need to know that it cannot guess?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which statements about a thread summary are true?
options: It can drop a condition attached to a decision
It can treat an early proposal as final after a later message changed it
It can attribute a task to the wrong person
It only leaves out small talk, so decisions are always safe
blocks.explanation: Compression loses conditions, changes and owners. Decisions are not safe by default.
blocks.hint: Think about what gets lost when many messages become a few lines.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this summary request most useful.
blocks.prompt: Summarize this thread for me. ___ Quote the sentence each item comes from.
options: Make it short.
List decisions made, questions still open, and the owner and date for each action.
Tell me what matters.
blocks.explanation: Named categories and quotes let you verify each item.
blocks.hint: Choose the request that gives the output a shape you could check.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Which Gemini features you can use depends on your account type and organization settings.
cards.explanation: Admins control features, so colleagues may differ.

cards.statement: A confident, well-organized summary does not need checking against the original.
cards.explanation: Summaries can swap names or dates and read smoothly.

cards.statement: When you rewrite a document for a new reader, you should say which facts must not change.
cards.explanation: Rewrites can shift numbers.

blocks.hint: Ask whether sounding right is the same as being right.

blocks.question: A drafted reply says "we will refund you within 5 days", but you never agreed to that. What do you do?
options: Send it, since the AI read the thread and probably saw a reason.
Remove the promise or confirm it with your team before sending.
Soften it to "soon".
blocks.explanation: You are committing. Keep only promises you made or approved.
blocks.hint: Who is responsible for what the email promises?

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give Gemini to reply to a message or rewrite a document, with made-up details only.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request asking Gemini to draft a reply or rewrite a text connected to this pain. Include the reader, the facts to keep, a note on your voice, and a length limit. Add one line on what you would verify before sending.
practice.default_context: A long email thread with a client about a delayed project needs a short reply that confirms a new date and keeps a friendly tone.

rubric.description: Names who reads it and the specific facts the draft must contain or keep.
Describes the tone, offers a style sample or limits the length.
Says which dates, amounts or commitments will be confirmed in the original.

practice.example_good_prompt: Reply to the client's last message. Match the warm, brief tone of my earlier email below. Confirm the new delivery date of 14 March, apologize once, no promises about compensation, under 90 words. Before sending I will check the date and that I made no new commitments.

common_mistakes: Learners ask for a reply with no facts. Ask what the reader needs to learn from the message.
Learners send summaries unchecked. Have them find one deadline in the original thread.
Learners let a draft make promises. Ask who approved each commitment.
key_points: Give a tone sample, the reader and the facts.
Ask for summaries in decisions, questions and owners.
Verify dates, amounts and commitments in the original.
follow_up_tasks: Summarize one real thread you know well and find one detail the summary got wrong or left out.

lessons.goal: Organize messy data, get formulas explained or written, run a quick analysis and spot-check the results.
lessons.title: Sheets: organize, explain, analyze

blocks.title: Organize messy data
blocks.body: Gemini can turn a rough list into a clean table or standardize names and dates. Describe one problem: "Column B has dates in three formats." Work in a copy.

blocks.title: Formulas explained or written
