blocks.body: Ask what an inherited formula does, step by step. Or describe the goal: "Add up column D where column B says Paid and column C is March." Name columns and conditions, then test on rows you can calculate by hand.

blocks.title: Analyze, then spot-check
blocks.body: Ask for trends or outliers. The answer may skip rows, misread a column or count twice. Compare the row count, recalculate one total, and check the highest and lowest values. Keep personal data such as salaries or grades in approved tools.

blocks.question: You inherit a sheet with a long formula you did not write. What is the best first request?
options: Rewrite this formula to make it shorter.
Explain this formula step by step, say what each column holds, and suggest two rows to test it on.
Fix any errors in this formula.
blocks.explanation: Understanding comes before changing. A step-by-step explanation lets you test the logic.
blocks.hint: What would you want to know before touching a formula you did not write?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Gemini says Marketing spent 12,400 across 45 rows. Which checks are useful?
options: Count the Marketing rows and compare with 45
Filter to Marketing and add up the amounts yourself
Accept it, since the sheet is open in front of the AI
Scan the largest and smallest amounts for typos such as an extra zero
blocks.explanation: Quick checks reveal skipped rows and typos.
blocks.hint: Pick the checks that only need the sheet and a minute.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this cleanup request work.
blocks.prompt: Column A holds customer names typed in different ways. ___ Leave all other columns untouched.
options: Tidy it up.
Suggest a formula that writes each name as First Last with no extra spaces, and list the entries it cannot handle.
Make the names look nicer.
blocks.explanation: A target format plus a list of exceptions shows what needs manual work.
blocks.hint: What would you want to know after Gemini has finished?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Asking Gemini to fix one named problem at a time is easier to review than "clean this sheet".
cards.explanation: Small, specific changes are easier to check.

cards.statement: A student gradebook with names is fine to analyze in any AI tool you find online.
cards.explanation: Student data belongs in tools your school approves.

cards.statement: If the AI's total differs from your own, the AI is probably right.
cards.explanation: Investigate the difference. Either of you may have skipped or misread rows.

blocks.hint: Think about what you can check and what stays private.

blocks.question: Gemini says column A holds 12 duplicate customers and offers to remove them. What do you do first?
options: Let it remove them, since it counted them.
Ask it to list them, then check a few in a copy of the sheet.
Remove them all and compare later.
blocks.explanation: Similar entries are not always duplicates. A listed sample in a copy lets you check first.
blocks.hint: What can you undo if the AI misjudged?

practice.instructions: Write a request asking Gemini for a formula, a cleanup or a quick analysis for a table from your work, and say how you will check it. Use made-up data.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request for Gemini about a spreadsheet related to this pain, or a made-up one that fits your work. Describe the columns, say what result you want back, and explain how you would spot-check it.
practice.default_context: A training sign-up sheet has columns for name, team, course and date. Names are typed inconsistently, and you need the number of sign-ups per course.

rubric.description: Names the columns and what each one holds.
Says exactly which formula, cleanup or analysis is needed.
Names a concrete check such as recalculating one total or comparing row counts.

practice.example_good_prompt: My sheet has A name, B team, C course, D date. Names in column A are typed in different ways. Suggest a formula that writes each as First Last and list the entries it cannot handle. Then count sign-ups per course. I will filter one course and count by hand.

common_mistakes: Learners describe the goal but not the columns. Ask what each column contains.
Learners accept totals unchecked. Have them recalculate one figure by hand.
Learners use real personal data. Point them to approved tools or made-up data.
key_points: Name columns, conditions and the result you want.
Work on a copy.
Spot-check counts, one total and the extremes.
follow_up_tasks: Ask Gemini to explain one formula from your own sheet, then reproduce its result on two rows by hand.

lessons.goal: Build a first presentation from your notes, find and summarize files across Drive, and keep track of the source files you rely on.
lessons.title: Slides and Drive: first drafts and file search

blocks.title: A first deck from your notes
blocks.body: Start with the audience and the one message they should leave with. Give Gemini your notes and ask for an outline first, then slides one section at a time. Tell it to use only your notes and mark gaps instead of inventing figures.

blocks.title: Find and summarize in Drive
blocks.body: Where your account allows it, Gemini can search files you can already open and summarize them: "What do our Q3 planning documents say about the training budget?" It may miss a file or pick an old version.

blocks.title: Reference your sources
blocks.body: Ask which files an answer used. Open them, find the passage, and keep the file names in your speaker notes. Before using a figure, confirm it in the file and check the file's date.

blocks.question: You want Slides for a team briefing based on a planning document. What is the best first request?
options: Turn this document into a 20-slide deck.
Suggest a five-section outline for a 15-minute team briefing from this document. Key message: the launch moves to May.
Make slides that look great.
blocks.explanation: An outline lets you agree the structure while changes are cheap.
blocks.hint: What do you want to agree on before any content is written?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Gemini summarized your Drive files on the training budget. What should you do before quoting it?
options: Ask which files it used
Open those files and find the passage
Check the date or version of each file
Trust it because it searched your own Drive
blocks.explanation: Searching your Drive does not guarantee the newest version or a correct reading.
blocks.hint: Which actions let you trace a claim back to a document?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this Drive question most trustworthy.
blocks.prompt: What do our planning documents say about the training budget? ___
options: Be thorough.
Name the file behind each point and tell me if documents disagree.
Include everything you can find.
blocks.explanation: File names let you open the source, and disagreements show where you must decide.
blocks.hint: Which request lets you trace each point back?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A Drive summary can miss a relevant file or use an outdated one.
cards.explanation: Check dates and look for gaps.

cards.statement: Asking Gemini to write [gap] where a figure is missing keeps unknowns visible.
cards.explanation: A visible gap is easy to fix. An invented figure looks like a fact.

cards.statement: Gemini can use any file in your organization to answer your question.
cards.explanation: It only uses files you can already open, and it may still miss some.

blocks.hint: Ask what Gemini can see, and what it might not tell you.

blocks.question: A slide says "attendance rose 12%", but you cannot find that number in your notes or files. What now?
options: Keep it, because it matches the trend you expected.
Remove it or find the source before presenting.
Rephrase it as "attendance rose significantly".
blocks.explanation: A claim with no source should not reach an audience. Softer wording still states an unsupported claim.
blocks.hint: Where would you point if someone asked for the source?

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give Gemini to outline a short presentation from your notes, and name the files you would verify. Use made-up details.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request that asks Gemini to turn rough notes into an outline for a short presentation about this topic. Include the audience, the key message, the number of sections and what Gemini should do about missing facts. Add a line on which source files you would open to verify the figures.
practice.default_context: You must brief your team on a project change in 15 minutes, using rough notes and a planning document in your Drive.

rubric.description: Says who will watch and what they should take away or decide.
Tells the AI to use only the notes and to mark missing facts.
Names the files or notes that will be checked before using any figure.

practice.example_good_prompt: Using only my pasted notes and the planning document, outline a 15-minute team briefing. Key message: the launch moves to May. Five sections, impact on each team first, mark missing facts as [gap]. Before presenting I will open the plan and confirm every date.

common_mistakes: Learners ask for a full deck at once. Steer them to outline first, then sections.
Learners trust Drive summaries. Ask which file and which passage each claim came from.
Learners skip the audience. Ask what the reader should decide.
key_points: Outline first, then slides, using only your notes.
Drive answers depend on your access and may use old files.
Name and open the sources behind every figure.
follow_up_tasks: Ask Gemini to summarize one folder topic, then open two cited files and note anything it missed.

courses.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot at Work
courses.description: Use Microsoft 365 Copilot to catch up on email and meetings, draft documents and presentations from your own files, and work with spreadsheet data, while checking every result.

lessons.goal: Summarize long email threads and chats, draft replies in your tone, and verify names, dates and commitments before acting.
lessons.title: Outlook and Teams: catch up fast

blocks.title: What Copilot sees
blocks.body: Microsoft 365 Copilot works with your own mail, chats, meetings and files, within the access you already have. What you can use depends on your company's license and settings. Ask IT what is switched on.

blocks.title: Summarize with a purpose
blocks.body: After leave or a missed meeting, ask a specific question: "What was decided, what is open, and what is assigned to me?" This beats "summarize". Name the thread, chat or meeting so Copilot looks in the right place. Meeting summaries need the meeting to have been transcribed, which your organization controls.

blocks.title: Draft in your voice, then check
blocks.body: Ask for a reply and describe your tone: "short, friendly, no jargon". Give the decision you want to communicate. Before sending, compare names, dates and promises against the original messages. A reply can commit you to something you never agreed to.

blocks.question: You return from two weeks off and face a 60-message project thread. Which request is most useful?
options: Summarize this thread.
List the decisions made, the questions still open, and anything assigned to me, with who said it.
Tell me what matters.
blocks.explanation: A specific question gives you decisions, open items and your own tasks, with names you can check.
blocks.hint: Which request tells Copilot what you will do with the answer?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Copilot drafted your reply to a client thread. What do you check before sending?
options: The delivery date it mentions
Whether the tone matches how you write
Any promise made on your behalf
Whether the draft is longer than the original
blocks.explanation: Dates, tone and promises can all be wrong. Length matters little next to commitments in your name.
blocks.hint: Think about what the client could hold you to.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this catch-up request work.
blocks.prompt: Summarize the Teams meeting I missed on Tuesday. ___ Quote the person who said it.
options: Make it interesting.
List only decisions and action items with owners and due dates.
Be brief.
blocks.explanation: Decisions, owners and dates are what you act on, and quotes let you verify them.
blocks.hint: Choose the instruction that names the output you need.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A meeting summary can attribute a task to the wrong person.
cards.explanation: Summaries can mix up speakers. Check owners before you act.

cards.statement: If Copilot summarizes a thread, you no longer need to read the last message.
cards.explanation: The latest message may change a decision. Read it yourself.

cards.statement: Copilot can only use what you have access to.
cards.explanation: It works within your permissions, so ask IT what is enabled for you.

blocks.hint: Ask what could be lost when a long conversation is shortened.

blocks.question: The summary says "the budget was approved by Dana for 20 March". What is your best next step?
options: Add it to your plan, since a summary is reliable.
Ask Copilot to confirm it is right.
Open the original message or recording and check who approved it and when.
blocks.explanation: Asking the same tool to confirm adds little. The source settles it.
blocks.hint: Where did the sentence originally come from?

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give Copilot to catch you up on a thread or meeting, and say how you would verify the answer. Use made-up details.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request asking Copilot to summarize a long email thread or a missed meeting related to this. Say what you want back (decisions, open questions, your tasks), and name one detail you would check in the original before acting.
practice.default_context: You were away for a week and need to catch up on a long email thread about a client event with several open decisions.

rubric.description: Says which thread, chat or meeting should be summarized.
Requests decisions, open questions, owners or deadlines instead of a general summary.
Names a concrete detail to verify in the original before acting.

practice.example_good_prompt: Summarize the email thread 'Spring client event' from the last two weeks. List decisions made, open questions, and anything assigned to me, with who said it. I will check the venue date and the budget figure in the original messages before replying.

common_mistakes: Learners ask for "a summary" with no goal. Ask what they will do with it.
Learners send drafted replies unchecked. Have them find every date and promise in the draft.
Learners assume Copilot sees everything. Remind them it depends on access and company settings.
key_points: Ask for decisions, open items and your tasks.
Describe your tone when drafting replies.
Verify names, dates and commitments in the source.
follow_up_tasks: Summarize one thread you know well and mark every fact the summary got wrong or left out.

lessons.goal: Draft from your own files, rewrite for an audience, turn a document into a presentation outline, and take ownership of the final version.
lessons.title: Word and PowerPoint: draft, rewrite, present

blocks.title: Draft from your own files
blocks.body: Point Copilot at the files that hold the facts: last year's report, a policy, meeting notes. Ask it to use only those sources and to mark gaps. Copilot only reads files you can open, but what you share can reveal their content to people who cannot.

blocks.title: Rewrite for the reader
blocks.body: One document often needs several versions. Ask for the same content rewritten for a manager, a client or a new colleague, with a length limit. Say what must stay unchanged, such as figures, names and deadlines.

blocks.title: From document to outline
blocks.body: Ask for an outline before slides: audience, one key message, five or six sections. Fix the structure, then ask for slides. Copilot's draft is a starting point. You own the final version, so read every slide aloud once.

blocks.question: You need a project status report. Which request keeps the draft closest to the facts?
options: Write a status report on our project.
Draft a status report using only the attached plan and meeting notes. Mark missing information as [gap].
Write an impressive status report.
blocks.explanation: Limiting the sources and marking gaps keeps invented details visible.
blocks.hint: Think about how you could tell what Copilot made up.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Copilot drafted a team update from files in several folders. What do you check before sending?
options: Whether it quotes details from files some recipients cannot open
Whether it includes confidential items, such as salaries or client data
Whether every figure matches its source file
Whether Copilot used files you cannot open
blocks.explanation: Copilot only uses files you can open, but your update can pass their content on.
blocks.hint: Who will read the update, and what can they already see?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that best completes this request.
blocks.prompt: Rewrite this process document for a colleague on their first day. ___ Keep every step and deadline unchanged.
options: Make it friendly.
Explain each abbreviation and give the steps as a numbered list, one sentence each.
Make it simpler.
blocks.explanation: Concrete rewrite instructions fit the reader. Fixed steps and deadlines keep the facts safe.
blocks.hint: Look for the option you could count when you read the result.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A draft from Copilot is ready to send as soon as it looks well written.
cards.explanation: Fluent text can still contain wrong figures or claims. Check it against your sources.

cards.statement: It is easier to fix a presentation's structure after Copilot has made all the slides.
cards.explanation: Changing an outline is cheap. Reworking finished slides is not.

cards.statement: If your name is on the document, you are responsible for what it says.
cards.explanation: The tool drafts, you decide. Responsibility stays with you.

blocks.hint: Think about who answers questions about the document later.

blocks.question: Copilot's slide says "Training completion reached 94%", but your source file says 84%. What do you do?
options: Keep it, since Copilot read your files.
Correct it from the file, then check the other figures on that slide too.
Ask Copilot whether it is sure.
blocks.explanation: One wrong figure suggests others. Fix it from the source and check the rest.
blocks.hint: What is the source of this number?

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give Copilot to draft a document or presentation outline from your own files. Use made-up file names and details.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request asking Copilot to draft a document, or turn a document into a presentation outline, related to this. Name the source files, the audience, the length, and what Copilot should do about missing facts.
practice.default_context: You must turn a 12-page process document into a one-page guide for new starters, using only what the document says.

rubric.description: Says which files or notes the draft must be based on.
States who reads it and asks for a length, outline or structure.
Tells Copilot to use only the sources and mark gaps, and says what you will check.

practice.example_good_prompt: Using only the file 'Onboarding process', draft a one-page guide for new starters. Plain language, numbered steps, keep every deadline as written, and mark anything unclear as [gap]. I will check each deadline against the document.

common_mistakes: Learners ask for a full deck at once. Steer them to an outline first.
Learners skip naming the source files. Ask where the facts should come from.
Learners polish the style and skip fact-checking. Have them trace two claims to the source.
key_points: Draft from named sources and mark gaps.
Say who reads it and what must stay unchanged.
You own the final version.
follow_up_tasks: Rewrite one paragraph for two readers and compare which facts each version put first.

lessons.goal: Get formulas explained or written, analyze a table and spot trends, then spot-check the results against the data.
lessons.title: Excel: formulas and data

blocks.title: Formulas in plain words
blocks.body: Ask Copilot to explain an inherited formula step by step. Or describe what you need: "Total the amounts in column C where column A is North and column B is March." Naming columns and conditions gives a formula you can test on rows you can calculate by hand.

blocks.title: Analyze a table
blocks.body: Copilot can summarize a table and point out trends and unusual values. Keep your data in a clear table with headers. Ask a specific question: "Which three products grew fastest from January to June?" Work on a copy for changes.

blocks.title: Spot-check the answer
blocks.body: Analysis can skip rows or misread a column. Check the row count, recalculate one total yourself and look at the highest and lowest values. For personal data such as salaries, follow your company's rules.

blocks.question: Copilot misreads your order list, which has blank rows, merged headers and typed subtotals. What is the best first step?
options: Ask the same question with more words.
Tidy it into one plain table with a single header row.
Delete the rows that look unusual.
blocks.explanation: A clear table gives Copilot less to misread. Unchecked deletions can remove real data.
blocks.hint: What makes a table easy for anyone to read?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Copilot says the North region total is 48,200 from 90 rows. Which checks make sense?
options: Count the North rows in your table and compare with 90
Filter to North and add up the amounts yourself
Look at the largest and smallest North amounts for an extra zero
Accept it, since Copilot works from your own workbook
blocks.explanation: Quick checks catch skipped rows and misread columns.
blocks.hint: Which checks use only your own sheet?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that best completes this request.
blocks.prompt: Explain the formula in cell E2. ___ Then show me how to test it on two rows.
options: Make it simple.
Go through it step by step and say what each part refers to.
Fix it.
blocks.explanation: A step-by-step explanation lets you judge whether the logic matches your intent.
blocks.hint: What do you need before you can judge a formula?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A trend Copilot reports should be confirmed against the numbers in your table.
cards.explanation: A trend is a claim about the data. You can check it.

cards.statement: Blank cells and mixed formats in a table never affect an analysis.
cards.explanation: Messy data can lead to skipped or miscounted rows. Tidy it first.

cards.statement: If a formula returns a number, it must be correct.
cards.explanation: A formula can run and still answer the wrong question. Test it on rows you know.

blocks.hint: Think about what a number proves by itself.

blocks.question: Copilot added a column with a new formula, and the totals look believable. What is the safest next step?
options: Send the sheet, since the totals look believable.
Test it on two or three rows you can calculate by hand.
Ask Copilot whether it is sure.
blocks.explanation: Believable is not correct. A hand calculation shows whether the formula answers your question.
blocks.hint: Which option gives you evidence instead of reassurance?

practice.instructions: Write the request you would give Copilot about a table from your work, and describe how you would check the answer. Use made-up data only.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a request asking Copilot for a formula, an explanation or a trend analysis for a table related to this, or a made-up table that fits your work. Describe the columns, say what result you want, and name a concrete spot-check.
practice.default_context: You have a table of monthly orders with columns for date, region, product and amount, and you need totals per region and the fastest-growing product.

rubric.description: Names the columns and what each one contains.
Says exactly which formula, total or trend is needed.
Names a concrete check such as a row count, a manual total or the highest and lowest values.

practice.example_good_prompt: My table has columns: A date, B region, C product, D amount. Give me a formula for total amount per region, and tell me which product grew fastest from January to June. I will check by filtering one region and adding it up, and by comparing the row count.

common_mistakes: Learners do not describe columns or conditions. Ask what each column holds.
Learners accept totals and trends unchecked. Have them recalculate one number.
Learners analyze messy tables without tidying. Suggest fixing headers and blanks first.
key_points: Describe columns, conditions and the result you want.
Ask for explanations of formulas you inherit.
Spot-check counts, one total and extremes.
follow_up_tasks: Ask Copilot to explain one formula from your own sheet, then rebuild its result on two rows by hand.

courses.title: Research with Sources
courses.description: Research a topic with AI, check every source it gives you and write a short brief where each claim can be traced to a real source.

lessons.goal: Ask an AI search assistant for a sourced answer and confirm that each citation exists and supports the claim.
lessons.title: Check the sources behind an AI answer

blocks.title: Ask for sources
blocks.body: AI search assistants look up web pages and link them in the answer. Ask a narrow question and request a source for every claim, like "What does the regulator say about data retention for small employers?"

blocks.title: Three ways a citation fails
blocks.body: The link may not exist. The page may not contain the claim. Or it says something close, such as another year or country. A link proves nothing until you open it.

blocks.title: Check in three steps
blocks.body: Open the link. Find the sentence the answer relies on. Compare numbers, dates and conditions word by word. Prefer the original source over a blog repeating it.

blocks.question: An AI search answer says a survey found 62% of employees prefer hybrid work, with a link. What do you do first?
options: Trust it, because a link is attached.
Open the link and find the 62% on the page.
Ask the assistant if the number is correct.
Check that the website looks professional.
blocks.explanation: Only the page itself shows whether the figure is there. Asking the assistant again is not a check.
blocks.hint: Where could you see the number with your own eyes?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which are ways a citation can fail?
options: The link leads to a page that does not exist.
The page exists but never mentions the claim.
The page covers a different year than the answer states.
The link opens a page from a well-known organization.
blocks.explanation: Missing pages, unsupported claims and mismatched details are common. A known publisher does not put the claim on the page.
blocks.hint: Think about what could differ between the answer and the page.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this question most useful for research.
blocks.prompt: What are the notice rules for ending a fixed-term lease in my country? ___
options: Answer briefly.
Give a link for each rule and say which page section it comes from.
Be confident.
blocks.explanation: Asking for a link and location per rule gives you something specific to open and check.
blocks.hint: Which option gives you something you can verify?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A citation can look real and still not support the claim.
cards.explanation: The page may say something different or nothing at all on the point.

cards.statement: If the link opens, the claim is confirmed.
cards.explanation: You still need to find the supporting sentence on the page.

cards.statement: An original source is better than a blog repeating it.
cards.explanation: Copies can add errors or leave out conditions.

cards.statement: Asking "are you sure?" checks a source.
cards.explanation: It may repeat the mistake. Open the page.

blocks.hint: Ask whether you saw the evidence yourself.

blocks.question: The answer says "the fee is 150 euros" and cites a page. The page says "up to 150 euros, depending on the size of the company." What is the problem?
options: None, the number matches.
The answer dropped a condition the page states.
The page is too short to be a source.
The assistant should have linked two pages.
blocks.explanation: The number matches, but "up to" and the condition change the meaning. Compare conditions, not only numbers.
blocks.hint: Compare everything the page says with the answer.

practice.instructions: Write a research question for an AI search assistant, then describe how you would check two of its citations.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a narrow question for {{tool}} (or another AI search assistant) about a topic related to this pain, and ask for a source per claim. Then describe how you would check two citations in its answer: what you would open and what you would compare.
practice.default_context: You are an office manager who needs to know how long a company must keep invoices and wants a sourced answer.

rubric.description: The question names the topic, place or time frame instead of asking for a general overview.
The prompt asks for a link or reference for each claim.
The learner opens the source, finds the sentence and compares numbers, dates or conditions.

practice.example_good_prompt: What is the minimum period a small company in Germany must keep invoices? Give each rule with a link to an official page and the section it comes from. Afterwards I will open two links, find the sentence about the period and compare the number of years and who the rule applies to.

common_mistakes: Learners treat a link as proof. Ask them to point to the sentence on the page.
Learners check only numbers. Ask about dates, places and conditions too.
key_points: A citation can be missing, unsupported or slightly different.
Open the source and compare word by word.
Prefer the original source.
follow_up_tasks: Take one sourced AI answer and mark each claim as confirmed, changed or not found.

lessons.goal: Ask an AI tool to answer only from documents you provide, with quotes and page references, and name what it cannot see.
lessons.title: Work from your own documents

blocks.title: Answers from your files
blocks.body: Source-grounded notebooks and chat assistants with file upload can answer from documents you give them, such as a contract, a policy or a set of reports. The answer should come from your files, not from memory.

blocks.title: Ask for quotes and pages
blocks.body: Add rules to your question: "Use only the uploaded files. Quote the exact sentence and give the page. If the files do not say, answer 'not in the documents.'" Then compare each quote with the page.

blocks.title: Know the blind spots
blocks.body: The tool sees only what you uploaded. Scanned pages, images, tables and charts may be read badly or skipped. Long files may be used only in part. Upload confidential files only if your company approves the tool.

blocks.question: You upload three vendor contracts and ask about the notice period. Which instruction best limits invention?
options: Tell me the usual notice period for vendors.
Use only these files. Quote the clause and page. If it is missing, say so.
Summarize everything you know about contracts.
Answer in one word.
blocks.explanation: It restricts the answer to your files, asks for evidence and gives a safe way to say "not found."
blocks.hint: What should the tool do if the clause is missing?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. What may a grounded tool miss in your uploads?
options: Text inside scanned images.
Numbers in complex tables.
A document you forgot to upload.
Plain text paragraphs in a readable file.
blocks.explanation: Scans, tables and missing files are common blind spots. Plain readable text is usually fine, but still check quotes.
blocks.hint: Think about what is hard to read or absent.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt safest.
blocks.prompt: Which deadlines are in the attached grant guidelines? ___
options: Add typical deadlines if they are missing.
List each deadline with an exact quote and page. If none is stated, write 'not in the documents.'
Give me a short and friendly answer.
blocks.explanation: Quotes and pages let you verify, and the fallback phrase stops the tool from guessing.
blocks.hint: What should happen when the guidelines say nothing?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: A tool that answers from your files can still misquote them.
cards.explanation: Always compare the quote with the original page.

cards.statement: If the answer is "not in the documents," the topic is not covered anywhere.
cards.explanation: It only means your uploaded files do not cover it.

cards.statement: Asking for page references makes checking faster.
cards.explanation: You can jump straight to the passage.

cards.statement: You can upload any client file to any tool.
cards.explanation: Use only tools your organization approves for confidential material.

blocks.hint: Think about what the tool knows and what it does not.

blocks.question: The tool quotes "payment within 30 days" and cites page 4. Page 4 says "payment within 14 days." What do you conclude?
options: Page 4 is probably a typo.
The quote is wrong, so do not use the answer.
Both numbers are acceptable.
The tool is right because it read the whole file.
blocks.explanation: A quote that does not match the page cannot be relied on. Check the other claims from the same answer too.
blocks.hint: What does the original page say?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that limits the tool to your documents, asks for quotes and pages, and says what to do when the answer is missing.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Imagine you uploaded two or three documents related to this pain into {{tool}}. Write a prompt that asks one question using only those documents, requires exact quotes and page references, and says what to answer if the documents do not say. Then name one thing the tool might not see.
practice.default_context: You are a teacher who uploaded the school's assessment policy and the exam schedule and wants to know the rules for retaking a test.

rubric.description: The prompt says to use only the provided documents.
The prompt requires exact quotes and page references.
The prompt gives a fallback answer and the learner names a blind spot, such as scans or tables.

practice.example_good_prompt: Use only the two uploaded documents. What are the rules for retaking a failed test? Quote each rule exactly and give the document and page. If the documents do not say, write 'not in the documents.' I know it may skip the tables in the exam schedule, so I will check those myself.

common_mistakes: Learners assume grounded means always correct. Ask them to compare one quote with the page.
Learners forget the fallback. Ask what the tool should say when the files are silent.
key_points: Limit the answer to your files.
Ask for quotes and pages.
Know what the tool cannot see.
follow_up_tasks: Upload one short document and check three quotes against the original.

lessons.goal: Separate facts from AI interpretation, handle sources that disagree and write a brief where every claim has a source.
lessons.title: Turn facts into a sourced brief

blocks.title: Facts and interpretation
blocks.body: A fact comes from a source: "The report states turnover rose 8%." Interpretation is the AI's reading: "This suggests customers are happier." Ask the assistant to label each statement as fact with source, or interpretation. Keep interpretation only if you agree and mark it as yours.

blocks.title: When sources disagree
blocks.body: Two sources give different numbers. Do not let the assistant average them. Ask it to list both, with date, author and method. Often one is newer, covers a different group or measures something else. If you cannot tell, report the range and say so.

blocks.title: The sourced brief
blocks.body: Write a short brief: one-sentence conclusion, three to five claims, each followed by its source. Delete any claim you could not verify. Ask the assistant to flag sentences without a source, then check them yourself.

blocks.question: Which sentence is an interpretation, not a fact?
options: The survey covered 400 teachers.
Absence rose from 4% to 6%, according to the HR report.
The rise shows that morale is falling.
The report was published in spring.
blocks.explanation: The report gives the numbers. The cause is a reading that the report does not state.
blocks.hint: Which sentence goes beyond what a source reports?

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Two sources give different market sizes. What should you ask?
options: Which source is newer?
Do they measure the same group or definition?
What method did each one use?
Which number is easier to remember?
blocks.explanation: Date, scope and method explain most differences. Memorability has nothing to do with accuracy.
blocks.hint: What could explain two honest numbers differing?

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this prompt most useful.
blocks.prompt: Here are my notes and two sources. Draft a brief for my manager. ___
options: Make it sound convincing.
Put the source after every claim and label any sentence that is your interpretation.
Add extra statistics to strengthen it.
blocks.explanation: It keeps each claim traceable and separates the facts from the assistant's reading.
blocks.hint: Which option protects you from unsupported claims?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: When two sources disagree, you should report both and explain the difference.
cards.explanation: Hiding a conflict makes your brief look more certain than the evidence is.

cards.statement: A claim you could not verify can stay if it sounds reasonable.
cards.explanation: Remove it or mark it clearly as unverified.

cards.statement: Asking the assistant to flag unsourced sentences helps your review.
cards.explanation: It shows where to look first, but you still verify.

cards.statement: An average of two conflicting figures is a safe compromise.
cards.explanation: The average matches neither source and may be wrong for both.

blocks.hint: Ask whether a reader could trace each claim.

blocks.question: Your draft brief has a strong sentence with no source. What is the best step?
options: Keep it, because the tone fits the brief.
Find a source for it, or delete it.
Cite the AI assistant as the source.
Move it to the end where it is less noticeable.
blocks.explanation: Every claim needs a source you have checked. Otherwise it should not be in the brief.
blocks.hint: What must a reader be able to do with each claim?

practice.instructions: Write a prompt that turns your sources into a short brief with a source for every claim, and explain how you would handle a conflict.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. You have collected two or three sources on a topic related to this pain and they partly disagree. Write a prompt for {{tool}} that produces a short brief with one conclusion and several claims, each with its source, and separates facts from interpretation. Then say how you would handle the disagreement and what you would check before sharing it.
practice.default_context: You are a marketing coordinator who must brief your manager on the size of a local market, but two reports give different figures.

rubric.description: The prompt requires a source after each claim and a flag on any unsourced sentence.
The prompt asks the assistant to label interpretation separately from facts.
The learner compares date, scope or method of the sources and plans to verify before sharing.

practice.example_good_prompt: Using only the two reports I pasted, write a brief for my manager: one-sentence conclusion, then four claims, each followed by its source. Label anything that is your interpretation. Where the reports give different market sizes, show both with year and method instead of choosing. Flag any sentence without a source. I will check each claim against the reports before sending.

common_mistakes: Learners blend interpretation into facts. Ask which sentence the source actually states.
Learners smooth over conflicts. Ask what differs in date, group or method.
key_points: Label facts and interpretation.
Show disagreement instead of hiding it.
Remove claims you cannot source.
follow_up_tasks: Take a paragraph from an AI summary and mark each sentence as fact, interpretation or unsourced.

courses.title: Safe AI at Work
courses.description: Decide what you can paste into an AI tool, remove identifying details before you prompt, and follow clear rules for responsible AI use at work.

lessons.goal: Sort your work information into four categories and decide which tool, if any, may receive it.
lessons.title: Know what you are pasting and where

blocks.title: Personal tool or company tool
blocks.body: A free personal AI account and a company-provided tool can look identical. Behind the screen, settings and contracts differ: what is stored, who can read it, and whether it helps train the service. You cannot see this in the chat window. Use the tools your company approves for work.

blocks.title: Four kinds of information
blocks.body: **Public:** already published, such as your website copy. **Internal:** meant for staff, such as a meeting agenda. **Confidential:** harmful if leaked, such as pricing, contracts or financials. **Personal data:** anything about an identifiable person, such as names, addresses or performance reviews. The higher the risk, the fewer tools may receive it.

blocks.title: A real example
blocks.body: A customer complaint names the customer and quotes their address. That is personal data. Do not paste it into a personal tool. In an approved tool, paste it only if your rules allow that category. If unsure, ask before you paste.

blocks.question: What is the most important difference between a personal AI account and a company-approved tool?
options: The approved tool always gives better answers.
Storage and contracts can differ, even if the screen looks the same.
Personal accounts are less accurate, which is the main risk.
There is no difference if you delete the chat afterwards.
blocks.explanation: Storage and use depend on the settings and agreements behind the tool, not on the screen.
blocks.hint: Think about what you can see in the chat window and what you cannot.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which of these are personal data?
options: A customer's home address in an email.
An employee's performance review.
Your company's published opening hours.
A student's grades with their name.
blocks.explanation: Each of these is about an identifiable person. Published opening hours describe the company, not a person.
blocks.hint: Ask whether the information is about a specific person you could name.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: If a tool looks professional, it is safe for confidential documents.
cards.explanation: Appearance says nothing about contracts or settings. Rely on your company's approval.

cards.statement: Internal information, such as a staff agenda, should stay out of personal AI accounts.
cards.explanation: Internal means meant for staff only, so it should not leave approved channels.

cards.statement: Information that is already public carries little risk in an AI tool.
cards.explanation: Public means anyone can already read it. Your own rules still come first.

blocks.hint: Separate how a tool looks from what the company has agreed with it.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes this habit safe.
blocks.prompt: Before I paste a document into an AI tool, I ___
options: check that the chat history is turned on.
check what kind of information it contains and whether my company allows it in this tool.
check that it is shorter than a page.
blocks.explanation: The information category and the tool's approval decide what is allowed.
blocks.hint: Which check depends on the information and the tool, not on the format?

blocks.question: Draft salary bands that only the leadership team has seen are which category?
options: Public
Internal, so any tool is fine
Confidential
No category, because there are no names
blocks.explanation: Leaked salary plans could harm the company and staff. Missing names do not make information harmless.
blocks.hint: Ask who would be affected if this document leaked.

practice.instructions: List three kinds of information from your work and sort each into a category, then say which you would never paste into a personal tool.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Name three pieces of information you handle while dealing with this pain. Sort each into public, internal, confidential or personal data. Then say which one you would never paste into a personal tool, and what you would check before using {{tool}} for the others.
practice.default_context: You are an office coordinator who handles customer emails, a staff rota and the company's price list.

rubric.description: Each item is placed in a sensible category with a short reason.
Personal or confidential items are identified as not suitable for a personal tool.
Mentions company rules, approved tools or asking a responsible person before pasting.

practice.example_good_prompt: 1) The published price page is public. 2) The staff rota is internal. 3) A customer email with an address is personal data. I would never paste the email into a personal tool. Before using any tool I would check our company rules and whether it is approved for that category.

common_mistakes: Learners judge a tool by how professional it looks. Ask what their company has approved.
Learners treat text without names as harmless. Ask who could be harmed if it leaked.
key_points: Settings and contracts differ between personal and approved tools.
Use four categories: public, internal, confidential, personal data.
When unsure, ask before pasting.
follow_up_tasks: Pick five documents from your last week and label each with a category.

lessons.goal: Rewrite a text so an AI tool can help without receiving details that identify a person or client.
lessons.title: Anonymize before you prompt

blocks.title: Replace the details
blocks.body: You rarely need real details to get help with wording. Replace names with placeholders like [Client]. Remove IDs and account numbers. Swap exact amounts for [Amount] or a range. Turn dates into "last month". Then add the real details back.

blocks.title: Names are not the only clue
blocks.body: A combination of facts can point to one person without a name. "The only part-time designer in the Northside office who joined last spring" identifies someone. So do a rare job title or a unique event. Look for details only one person or client could match.

blocks.title: A before and after
blocks.body:
Before: "Maria Lopez, account 48213, owes 2,300 and missed the 3 March deadline."

After: "A long-standing client owes [Amount] and missed a recent deadline. Draft a polite reminder."

The task is unchanged. Read your version as a stranger would. Could you guess who it is about? If yes, remove more.

blocks.question: Which version is the safest to paste into a personal AI tool?
options: Draft a reminder to Maria Lopez about invoice 48213.
Draft a reminder to M. L. about her late invoice.
Draft a reminder to a client about a late invoice. Use [Name] and [Amount].
Draft a reminder to the client in apartment 5 about invoice 48213.
blocks.explanation: Only the third removes the name and number and keeps placeholders.
blocks.hint: Check each option for a name, a number or a place.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. Which details could still identify someone after the name is removed?
options: Their exact job title in a very small team.
A unique event only they attended.
A general label such as 'a client'.
Their employee ID.
blocks.explanation: Rare titles, unique events and IDs point to one person. A general word like client does not.
blocks.hint: Think about which details only one person could match.

blocks.question: Pick the phrase that makes the prompt safe and still useful.
blocks.prompt: Summarize this complaint and suggest a reply. ___
options: The customer is John Reid from Dock Street.
The customer is [Customer]; the order was [Order] and the amount was [Amount].
The customer is the regular who always orders the oak table on Fridays.
blocks.explanation: Placeholders keep the task, not the identity.
blocks.hint: Which option gives the tool the task but not the person?

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: Removing the name is always enough to anonymize a text.
cards.explanation: Combinations of details can still point to one person or client.

cards.statement: You can add the real details back after the AI gives you a draft.
cards.explanation: Placeholders let you fill in names and numbers yourself.

cards.statement: Rounding an exact amount can reduce what a text reveals.
cards.explanation: Exact amounts can be matched to a record. A range is harder to match.

blocks.hint: Ask whether the detail changes the help you want or only reveals who is involved.

blocks.question: After anonymizing, what is a good final check?
options: Ask the AI whether it can identify the person.
Read the text as a stranger and see if you could guess who it is about.
Check that every placeholder uses the same brackets.
Check that the text is short.
blocks.explanation: A stranger test catches combinations of details.
blocks.hint: Whose view matters when judging if someone is identifiable?

practice.instructions: Rewrite a realistic work message so it can be pasted safely, then write the prompt you would send.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Invent a short realistic message or note related to this pain that contains a name, an amount, a date and one unique detail. Show the anonymized version, then write the prompt you would send to {{tool}}.
practice.default_context: A manager asks you to reply to a client named Sam Parker, account 77120, who disputes a 1,450 charge from 12 May after a unique on-site visit.

rubric.description: Names, IDs, exact amounts and exact dates are replaced with placeholders or general wording.
Details that only one person or client could match are removed or generalized.
The final prompt still states what the tool should produce, such as tone and length.

practice.example_good_prompt: A client disputes a recent charge of [Amount] after a service visit. Write a calm reply of under 100 words that acknowledges the concern, explains that we will review the details and asks for [Information needed]. I will add names and figures myself.

common_mistakes: Learners delete only the name. Ask which other details point to the same person.
Learners make the prompt too vague to be useful. Show how to keep the task and drop the identity.
key_points: Replace names, IDs, amounts and dates with placeholders.
Unique combinations of facts can still identify someone.
Read the result as a stranger would.
follow_up_tasks: Anonymize a real email from your inbox and ask a colleague to guess who it is about.

lessons.goal: Apply company rules, decide when to disclose AI use or avoid it, and respond properly when AI output causes a mistake.
lessons.title: Set your own rules for AI at work

blocks.title: Policy first
blocks.body: Your company's rules come before any tip you read. Follow the policy and use only approved tools, even when a personal tool is faster. If you cannot find a policy, ask your manager or IT team. No rule is not the same as permission.

blocks.title: Be open when it matters
blocks.body: Say when AI helped if it affects trust or decisions: client deliverables, assessed work, or anything your rules require. You need not announce every rewritten sentence. If asked, answer honestly. You remain responsible for what you send.

blocks.title: When not to use AI
blocks.body: Do not use AI when rules forbid it, when you cannot remove sensitive details, or to make a decision about a person, such as hiring or grading. A person with authority must decide.

blocks.title: When it goes wrong
blocks.body: If AI output caused a mistake, act quickly. Tell your manager or the affected person, and correct the error. Report accidentally shared sensitive data to whoever handles data at your company.

blocks.question: Your company has no written AI policy. What should you do?
options: Assume it is allowed.
Ask your manager or IT team what is allowed before you use AI for work data.
Use a personal tool, since no rule forbids it.
Wait and see.
blocks.explanation: A missing policy is not permission. Asking first protects everyone.
blocks.hint: Consider who can tell you what the company accepts.

blocks.question: Select all that apply. In which situations should you avoid AI or get approval first?
options: Rejecting a candidate based only on an AI summary.
Rewriting a public blog post for tone.
Your policy forbids AI for the client contract you are drafting.
You cannot remove personal data from the text.
blocks.explanation: Decisions about people, forbidden uses and unprotectable data rule AI out. A public post is low risk.
blocks.hint: Look for situations involving a person's outcome, a rule or data you cannot protect.

blocks.question: Swipe right if true, left if false.

cards.statement: You are responsible for AI-assisted work you send under your name.
cards.explanation: You are accountable, not the tool.

cards.statement: You must announce every sentence an AI rephrased.
cards.explanation: Disclose when trust, decisions or rules require it.

cards.statement: Fixing a data mistake quietly is better than reporting it.
cards.explanation: Early reporting lets the right people limit harm.

blocks.hint: Ask who is accountable and who needs to know.

blocks.question: Pick the best first step after you notice an AI-generated error in a sent report.
blocks.prompt: I will ___
options: wait to see if anyone notices.
tell my manager and the recipient, send a correction and note what happened.
delete the AI chat and say nothing.
blocks.explanation: Prompt disclosure and a correction reduce harm. Hiding the error makes it worse.
blocks.hint: Who needs to know, and how soon?

blocks.question: A teacher uses AI to draft feedback comments. Which use is appropriate?
options: Let the AI decide each student's final grade.
Use AI to suggest wording, then review the comments and decide the grade yourself.
Paste each student's full name and record into a personal tool.
Send the AI comments without reading them.
blocks.explanation: AI helps with wording; the teacher checks and decides. The others hand over a decision or expose data.
blocks.hint: Which option keeps the decision with a person and the data protected?

practice.instructions: Write a short personal AI rulebook for your work with at least four rules.
practice.task_template: You work as {{role}}. One of your daily pains is {{pain}}. Write a personal rulebook of four to five rules for using {{tool}} safely for this part of your work. Cover company policy, disclosure, a situation where you would not use AI, and what you would do after a mistake.
practice.default_context: You are an office administrator who starts using AI to draft emails and summarize documents.

rubric.description: At least one rule says to follow company policy or ask when unsure.
Includes when to say AI was used and a situation where AI is not used.
Names concrete steps after an error, such as telling the right person and correcting it.

practice.example_good_prompt: 1) I follow my company's AI rules and ask my manager when something is unclear. 2) I say when AI helped on client work or when I am asked. 3) I never use AI for decisions about individual people. 4) I remove personal details before pasting. 5) If AI output causes a mistake, I tell my manager, correct it and note what happened.

common_mistakes: Learners treat a missing policy as permission. Steer them to ask first.
Learners hide errors to avoid blame. Explain that early reporting limits harm.
key_points: Company rules come first.
Disclose AI use when it affects trust or decisions.
People decide about people, and mistakes are reported early.
follow_up_tasks: Find out who owns AI rules at your company and write down their name and contact.
